n: Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)

how.us_nsa: Paid for the National Student Association's international programme from the early 1950s until 1967, as Ramparts revealed in February 1967.
how.asia_foundation: Ran the Committee for a Free Asia, renamed the Asia Foundation in 1954, which the State Department calls a 'CIA proprietary'.
how.ccf: Founded and funded the Congress for Cultural Freedom from 1950 to 1966; the officer in charge, Thomas Braden, admitted it in 1967.
how.rferl: Paid for Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty in secret until 1972, when Congress took over the funding.
how.ftuc: Channelled money to the AFL's Free Trade Union Committee for about 20 years from 1948, starting with the Italian election.
how.ibad: Its link to IBAD, which ran anti-Goulart candidates in Brazil's 1962 election, was later confirmed; US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted $1-5 million was spent.
how.cia_front_network: Set up and paid the conduit foundations and front groups run by its International Organizations Division.
how.cia_bnd_rubicon: Bought the Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG in secret with the BND in 1970 for $5.75 million, and owned it alone from about 1993 to 2018.
how.gladio: Organised and supported stay-behind networks in western Europe, including West German ones in 1949-53, and sat in NATO stay-behind meetings.
how.ford_foundation: Used the Ford Foundation as a pass-through and cover for its money in the Cold War; chairman John J. McCloy (1958-65) set up a three-person committee to handle CIA requests, and in 1950 the foundation gave $150,000 to the CIA-controlled KgU in West Berlin.

d: The CIA is the United States' foreign spy service. During the Cold War it secretly paid for a large set of private-looking bodies: a student union, a labour committee, an Asian foundation, a writers' congress, two radio stations, a Brazilian election institute and a Swiss cipher company that sold coding machines to more than 120 countries. The money let it steer these bodies and, through them, the people and governments they reached, while each looked independent. Most of it came out through the 1967 Ramparts exposé, a 1966 New York Times series, Senate hearings in 1971, and, for Crypto AG, a 2020 report by the Washington Post, ZDF and SRF.
cite: Ramparts (1967); New York Times series (April 1966); Thomas Braden, Saturday Evening Post (1967); Washington Post/ZDF/SRF, 'The intelligence coup of the century' (11 Feb 2020); Lincoln Gordon interviews (1977, 1994); Frances Stonor Saunders, The Cultural Cold War (1999); Wikipedia, Ford Foundation

n: Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND, German foreign intelligence)

how.cia_bnd_rubicon: Co-owned Crypto AG with the CIA from its secret purchase in June 1970 until it sold out in about 1993.
how.crypto_ag: The BND bought Crypto AG in June 1970 for CHF 25 million and passed half to the CIA; the two secretly owned it until the BND sold its share to the CIA in 1994, and rigged its machines to read other states' messages.

d: The BND is West Germany's, and now Germany's, foreign intelligence service. In 1970 it and the CIA secretly bought Crypto AG, a Swiss company that sold encryption machines to governments around the world. Because the two agencies owned the firm, they could have its machines built so that they could read the messages of the countries that bought them. The BND sold its share to the CIA around 1993. The arrangement, called Thesaurus and later Rubicon, was revealed on 11 February 2020 by the Washington Post, the German broadcaster ZDF and Swiss broadcaster SRF, using the agencies' own internal histories.
cite: Washington Post, ZDF and SRF joint investigation (11 Feb 2020); Swiss parliamentary inquiry (2020); Washington Post and ZDF (11 Feb 2020); Crypto Museum Operation Rubicon file; Swiss parliamentary inquiry (2020)

n: US Agency for International Development (USAID) and predecessors

how.aifld: Provided most of AIFLD's money from the 1960s, later joined by the National Endowment for Democracy.
how.chile_project: US aid funding set up the first wave (1955-1964) of the Chicago-Catholic University exchange that trained the 'Chicago Boys'.
how.hiid: Paid HIID about $40 million without competitive bidding to advise Russia's privatisation in 1992-97; it cut the grant in 1997 and the US government later won $26.5 million from Harvard.

d: USAID is the US government's foreign aid agency, created in 1961 out of earlier aid offices. It paid most of the running costs of the American Institute for Free Labor Development, which the AFL-CIO set up in 1961 to train Latin American union leaders to oppose left-wing unions; a US Comptroller General report and congressional sources documented the funding. Earlier US aid money set up the programme that sent Chilean economics students to the University of Chicago from 1955. Those graduates later ran Chile's economy under Pinochet. In both cases public aid money built groups that then worked inside other countries' unions and ministries.
cite: US Comptroller General report on AIFLD funding; SourceWatch, AIFLD; Valdés, 'Pinochet's Economists' (1995); US General Accounting Office report (1996); US v. President and Fellows of Harvard College settlement (Aug 2005)

n: Rockefeller family and Rockefeller Foundation

how.trilateral: David Rockefeller was the principal founder of the Trilateral Commission in July 1973.
how.cfr: David Rockefeller chaired the Council on Foreign Relations in the 1970s; the Rockefeller Foundation fully paid for its secret War and Peace Studies in the Second World War.
how.ipr: The Rockefeller Foundation was the largest of the philanthropies that funded the Institute of Pacific Relations.
how.chile_project: The Rockefeller Foundation, with the Ford Foundation, funded the wider 'Chile Project'.
how.group_of_thirty: The Rockefeller Foundation initiated and paid for the founding of the Group of Thirty in 1978.

d: The Rockefellers built a fortune on Standard Oil and turned part of it into foundations. David Rockefeller, a banker who ran Chase Manhattan, founded the Trilateral Commission in 1973 and chaired the Council on Foreign Relations, two clubs where bankers, executives and future ministers meet. The Rockefeller Foundation paid for the Council's wartime planning studies, much of the Institute of Pacific Relations' budget and part of the Chicago training of Chilean economists. That money and leadership gave the family a say in who sat in these forums and what they studied. The links are on public record in the bodies' own histories and the foundation's grant reports.
cite: Trilateral Commission history; Council on Foreign Relations history (War and Peace Studies); Rockefeller Foundation records; Rockefeller Brothers Fund, 'RBF at 75'; Group of Thirty history

n: Koch network (Charles Koch foundations and Koch Industries)

how.alec: Koch foundations paid ALEC about $3.89 million in 1997-2019, lent it money in the 1990s, and a Koch lobbyist has sat on its corporate board every year since at least 1996.
how.atlas_network: Koch foundations gave Atlas Network between about $0.4 million and $0.7 million from 1987 onwards, according to Greenpeace and tax filings.
how.federalist_society: Koch family foundations were early donors to the Federalist Society.

d: Koch Industries is one of the largest private companies in the United States, run by Charles Koch, who with his late brother David funded a large network of foundations and political groups. Through those foundations and the company itself, the Kochs have paid for ALEC, where company lobbyists and state legislators draft model bills together, and given to the Atlas Network of free-market think tanks and the Federalist Society of conservative lawyers. A Koch lobbyist has held a seat on ALEC's corporate board since at least 1996. The figures come from the groups' tax returns, ALEC's own board minutes, and databases kept by Greenpeace and DeSmog.
cite: KochDocs, 'Koch Industries and ALEC: a history of documents' (2019); Greenpeace USA Koch database; IRS 990 filings; DeSmog, Atlas Network profile

n: Richard Mellon Scaife and the Scaife foundations

how.heritage_foundation: Became Heritage's primary donor about a year after its 1973 founding and gave tens of millions over two decades.
how.atlas_network: The Sarah Scaife Foundation gave Atlas Network about $2.37 million.
how.federalist_society: Was among the Federalist Society's early donors.
how.pnac: The Sarah Scaife Foundation gave grants to the Project for the New American Century.

d: Richard Mellon Scaife (1932-2014) was an heir to the Mellon banking and oil fortune. Through the Sarah Scaife Foundation and other family trusts he became one of the main paymasters of the American conservative movement. He was the Heritage Foundation's biggest donor in its first two decades, giving tens of millions of dollars, and his foundations also paid the Atlas Network and the Federalist Society. That money helped these groups grow from small offices into bodies that supply staff, policy papers and judges to US governments. The grants appear in the foundations' tax filings and in histories of the groups.
cite: Heritage Foundation history; Daily Signal (12 June 2024); DeSmog Atlas Network recipient table; Federalist Society donor records; Media Transparency grant records; IRS Form 990 filings

n: Joseph Coors and the Adolph Coors Foundation

how.heritage_foundation: Gave $250,000 in 1973, the first money the Heritage Foundation received, and kept funding it through the Adolph Coors Foundation.

d: Joseph Coors (1917-2003) was an heir to the Coors brewing company in Colorado. In 1973 he gave $250,000 to start the Heritage Foundation, a Washington think tank, and his family foundation kept funding it afterwards. Heritage went on to write policy blueprints for Republican administrations, from 'Mandate for Leadership' under Reagan to Project 2025, and to place its people in government posts. Coors's starting gift is recorded in Heritage's own history and in the Philanthropy Roundtable's account of its founding.
cite: Philanthropy Roundtable, 'Joe Coors brews up the Heritage Foundation'; Heritage Foundation history

n: John M. Olin Foundation

how.federalist_society: Gave the Federalist Society about $5.5 million in its early decades.
how.pnac: Gave grants to the Project for the New American Century.

d: The John M. Olin Foundation was set up by an arms and chemicals industrialist and spent its money on conservative ideas, especially in law schools, before closing in 2005 as planned. It gave the Federalist Society about $5.5 million, helping it grow from student chapters into a national network of lawyers. Federalist Society members later filled federal judgeships, including seats on the Supreme Court, and Justice Department posts. The grants are recorded in the foundation's reports and in histories of the society.
cite: Federalist Society history; John M. Olin Foundation grant records; Media Transparency grant records; IRS Form 990 filings

n: Leonard Leo network (Marble Freedom Trust), funded by Barre Seid

how.federalist_society: Leonard Leo, long its executive vice-president, became co-chairman of the Federalist Society in 2020; his Marble Freedom Trust received $1.6 billion from Barre Seid in 2021.

d: Leonard Leo is a lawyer who for decades ran the Federalist Society's day-to-day work and helped choose judges for Republican presidents. In 2020 he became its co-chairman. In 2021 Barre Seid, a Chicago electronics manufacturer, gave his whole company, worth about $1.6 billion, to the Marble Freedom Trust, a non-profit Leo chairs. It is the largest known political donation in US history. The money lets Leo's network fund groups that pick, promote and defend conservative judges. The gift came to light in August 2022 through tax documents obtained by the New York Times and ProPublica.
cite: New York Times and ProPublica (22 Aug 2022); Marble Freedom Trust tax filings; Federalist Society board records

n: George Soros and Open Society Foundations

how.cap: Promised up to $3 million when the Center for American Progress was set up in 2003.
how.riia: Open Society Foundations is listed among Chatham House's funders and partners.
how.onewest: Was one of the seven investors in IMB HoldCo, which bought the failed IndyMac from the FDIC in 2009 and ran it as OneWest Bank.

d: George Soros is a US hedge-fund billionaire whose Open Society Foundations fund liberal causes around the world. In 2003 he promised up to $3 million to start the Center for American Progress, a Washington think tank founded by John Podesta that later sent many staff into Democratic administrations. Open Society is also among the funders of Chatham House in London. Such money gives a donor a part in setting the agenda of the forums where policy is drafted. The pledges are reported in the bodies' donor lists and in press coverage at the time.
cite: The Nation, 'An idea factory for the Democrats' (2004); Center for American Progress donor list; Chatham House funding list; FDIC press release on IndyMac sale (19 March 2009)

n: Larry Ellison and the Larry Ellison Foundation

how.tbi: Has given or pledged at least £257 million to the Tony Blair Institute since 2021.

d: Larry Ellison co-founded the database company Oracle and is one of the world's richest people. Since 2021 his foundation has given or promised at least £257 million to the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, making him by far its biggest known funder. The institute advises governments in many countries on digital services and technology, fields in which Oracle sells products. The scale of the money, and what it means for the advice the institute gives, was set out by Lighthouse Reports and the New Statesman in September 2025.
cite: Peter Geoghegan and May Bulman, New Statesman (24 Sep 2025); Lighthouse Reports (2025)

n: William Volker Fund

how.mont_pelerin: Through its director Harold Luhnow, paid to bring American economists to the founding meeting of the Mont Pelerin Society in 1947.

d: The William Volker Fund was a charity built on a Kansas City furniture fortune and run from the 1940s by Harold Luhnow, who used it to spread free-market economics. It paid the travel of American participants to the first meeting of the Mont Pelerin Society in Switzerland in April 1947, the gathering Friedrich Hayek called to rebuild liberal economics. The society's members later became advisers, central bankers and ministers in many countries. The fund's role is recorded in the society's own histories and Bruce Caldwell's account of the founding.
cite: Bruce Caldwell, 'Mont Pelerin 1947' (Hoover Institution, 2022); Philanthropy Roundtable, William Volker Fund

n: Credit Suisse (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt)

how.mont_pelerin: Paid about 93 per cent of the cost of the 1947 founding conference, 18,062 Swiss francs.
how.greensill: Its supply-chain finance funds bought the notes that financed Greensill Capital; investors faced losses of up to $3 billion when Greensill collapsed in 2021.

d: Credit Suisse was one of Switzerland's two largest banks until UBS took it over in 2023. In 1947, as the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, it paid almost all the costs of the meeting that founded the Mont Pelerin Society. Seventy years later its asset-management arm ran the supply-chain finance funds that bought the debt notes on which Greensill Capital ran; when Greensill failed in March 2021, the bank estimated its fund investors could lose up to $3 billion. Both links are documented, the first in conference accounts, the second in the bank's own reports.
cite: Caldwell, 'Mont Pelerin 1947'; Credit Suisse Greensill report (2021); Financial Times (2020-21); Wall Street Journal (March 2021)

n: SoftBank Group and SoftBank Vision Fund

how.greensill: The Vision Fund invested $800 million in Greensill in 2019, and SoftBank put about $1.5 billion into the Credit Suisse funds that financed it.
how.uber: Became one of Uber's largest shareholders through a stake bought in 2018.

d: SoftBank is a Japanese technology investor led by Masayoshi Son. Its Vision Fund, which received a $45 billion commitment from Saudi Arabia's state fund, invested $800 million in Greensill Capital in 2019; SoftBank also put money into the Credit Suisse funds that bought Greensill's notes, at Lex Greensill's request, reported at about $1.5 billion. In 2018 it bought a large stake in Uber. Big shareholdings of this kind give an investor board influence and let it shape where a company grows. The Greensill sums were reported by the Financial Times and the Wall Street Journal in 2020-21.
cite: Financial Times (June 2020); Wall Street Journal (March 2021); SoftBank annual reports

n: Public Investment Fund (Saudi sovereign wealth fund)

how.uber: Invested $3.5 billion in Uber in 2016 and gained a seat on its board.
how.bk_softbank: Committed $45 billion to the SoftBank Vision Fund, its largest backer.

d: The Public Investment Fund is Saudi Arabia's state investment fund, with about $900 billion in assets, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. In 2016 it put $3.5 billion into Uber, which brought a seat on Uber's board for its governor, Yasir Al-Rumayyan. It also promised $45 billion to SoftBank's Vision Fund, which in turn invested in companies such as Greensill and Uber. Through these stakes the Saudi state became an owner, and a voice in the boardroom, of firms that lobby governments worldwide. The investments were publicly announced by the fund and the companies.
cite: Uber and PIF announcements (June 2016); SoftBank Vision Fund disclosures (2017); PIF annual reports

n: Russian presidency (Kremlin)

how.wagner: Putin said in June 2023 that the state paid Wagner 86.26 billion roubles (about $1 billion) between May 2022 and May 2023 and 'fully funded' it.
how.rostec: Putin signed the 2007 law creating Rostec; it is 100 per cent state-owned and its board and director are appointed by the president.
how.medvedchuk_network: Putin is godfather to Medvedchuk's daughter; Russia took Medvedchuk in a September 2022 prisoner exchange and he has lived in Moscow since.
how.russian_intel: The FSB and GRU answer to the president.
how.bk_promsvyazbank: The state took over Promsvyazbank in 2018 and made it the bank of the defence industry by law in 2019.
how.fsb: The FSB director is appointed by and answers directly to the Russian president, under a 2000 decree; Vladimir Putin ran the FSB in 1998-99 before becoming president.
how.gazprom: Owns just over half of Gazprom through the Federal Agency for State Property Management (38.4%) and Rosneftegaz (11%), and the Kremlin appoints its board chairs and chief executive.

d: The Russian presidency under Vladimir Putin sits at the top of the state bodies that run Russia's influence work abroad. Putin admitted in June 2023 that the state had paid for the Wagner mercenary group in full, about $1 billion in one year, after years of denying any link. He created the arms conglomerate Rostec by law in 2007 and appoints its leaders. He is a family friend of the Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk, whom Russia brought to Moscow in a 2022 prisoner swap. The spy services and the state bank Promsvyazbank also answer to him. Most of these facts come from Putin's own statements and Russian law.
cite: Putin remarks reported by Moscow Times (27 June 2023); Federal Law on Rostec (2007); Meduza (19 Feb 2021); Kyiv Independent; Wikipedia, Federal Security Service (citing presidential decrees); Gazprom annual reports; Federal Agency for State Property Management (Rosimushchestvo) records

n: Promsvyazbank (PSB)

how.shor_network: Moldovan police said $39 million reached about 138,000 Moldovan voters' accounts through PSB in September-October 2024, in a scheme run by Ilan Shor.

d: Promsvyazbank is a Russian bank owned by the state since 2018 and, by a 2019 law, the official bank of the defence industry. In October 2024 Moldovan police said that Ilan Shor, a fugitive businessman living in Russia, had used PSB to send $39 million to about 138,000 Moldovans in September and October, ahead of the presidential election and EU referendum, to pay them to vote as told and to campaign. Shor had already been sentenced in absentia to 15 years for a $1 billion bank fraud. Police released the account findings, though they had not yet published direct proof of each vote bought.
cite: Moldovan National Police statements reported by RFE/RL (25 Oct 2024); Promsvyazbank state ownership law (2018, 2019)

n: Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Concord group

how.wagner: Prigozhin was Wagner's owner and main funder until his death in 2023; Concord earned a further 80 billion roubles from army catering in 2022-23.
how.prigozhin_influence: A 2018 US indictment alleged Concord began operating in 2014 to finance the Internet Research Agency; the case against the company was dropped in 2020.

d: Yevgeny Prigozhin was a St Petersburg restaurateur who grew rich on state catering contracts through his Concord companies. He owned and paid for the Wagner Group of mercenaries and ran 'troll factories' and political consultants who worked on elections in the United States and Africa. Putin said Concord earned 80 billion roubles from army meals in a single year. A US grand jury charged Concord in 2018 with financing the Internet Research Agency; prosecutors later dropped the charge against the company to protect classified evidence. Prigozhin led a mutiny in June 2023 and died in a plane crash two months later.
cite: US v. Internet Research Agency et al., indictment (16 Feb 2018); Putin remarks (27 June 2023); Financial Times

n: GRU (Russian military intelligence)

how.marsalek_network: Jan Marsalek, suspected of working for the GRU and FSB, ran a Bulgarian spy ring in Britain whose six members were jailed in May 2025.

d: The GRU is Russia's military intelligence service. Jan Marsalek, the former operating chief of the German payments company Wirecard, fled to Russia in 2020 when Wirecard collapsed. Investigations by The Insider, Der Spiegel and others describe him as a GRU asset for a decade and report visits to FSB headquarters. From Russia he directed a ring of Bulgarians in Britain who spied on journalists and plotted kidnappings for Russian intelligence. A London jury convicted the ring in March 2025, and its six members were sentenced to about 50 years in total in May 2025.
cite: R v Roussev and others, Central Criminal Court (verdict 7 Mar 2025, sentence May 2025); The Insider and Der Spiegel investigations (2024); The Record (May 2025)

n: FSB (Russian Federal Security Service)

how.cybercrime_groups: The US Justice Department said in 2019 that Evil Corp leader Maksim Yakubets had worked for the FSB.
how.marsalek_network: Der Spiegel, ZDF and others reported in 2025 that Marsalek made visits to FSB headquarters in Moscow.

d: The FSB is Russia's main security service, successor to the KGB at home. When the United States sanctioned and charged the ransomware group Evil Corp in December 2019, the Justice Department said its leader, Maksim Yakubets, had worked for the FSB and was applying for a licence to handle state secrets. This means the state protects some criminal hackers who steal from banks and companies abroad and may use them. Reporting in 2025 also tied the fugitive Wirecard executive Jan Marsalek, who ran a spy ring in Britain, to FSB headquarters.
cite: US Department of Justice and Treasury announcements (5 Dec 2019); RFE/RL (2019); Der Spiegel/ZDF (2025)

n: Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party

how.ufwd: The United Front Work Department is an organ of the Central Committee and reports to it.
how.ccp_party_committees: Party rules require party committees in companies; at Huawei the chief ethics officer is also its party committee secretary.
how.confucius_institute: The Confucius Institute headquarters council was chaired by Politburo member Liu Yandong, a former head of the United Front Work Department.
how.bk_pla_liaison: The Central Military Commission, which commands the army's Political Work Department, is a party body.
how.mss: The Ministry of State Security sits under the party's Central National Security Commission and Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission, though formally a State Council ministry since 1983.
how.prc_talent_programs: The Central Committee and State Council raised the Thousand Talents Plan (announced 2008) to a national programme in 2010; the United Front Work Department's Western Returned Scholars Association represents its 7,000-plus recruits.

d: The Central Committee is the top body of the Chinese Communist Party, led by Xi Jinping. The United Front Work Department, which wins over and organises people and groups abroad, is one of its departments; in 2018 it absorbed the offices for overseas Chinese and religious affairs, and its affiliated bodies were estimated to spend at least $2.6 billion in 2019. The party also places committees inside companies and appoints the leaders of state programmes such as the Confucius Institutes. Xi calls united front work one of the party's 'magic weapons'. These lines of command appear in party rules and official announcements.
cite: CCP Central Committee institutional reform plan (March 2018); US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (2018); Huawei disclosures; Wikipedia, Ministry of State Security (China); Wikipedia, Thousand Talents Plan

n: Ministry of Education of China (via Hanban and the Chinese International Education Foundation)

how.confucius_institute: Funded Confucius Institutes through Hanban, and since 2020 through the Chinese International Education Foundation; US institutes usually received $100,000 a year.

d: China's Ministry of Education ran the Confucius Institute programme through Hanban, an agency under its control, until 2020, when the work passed to the Chinese International Education Foundation, also under the ministry. The institutes sit inside foreign universities and teach Chinese language and culture. China shares their costs with the host university; American institutes normally got $100,000 a year, and more than $150 million went to US universities between 2006 and 2019. Critics and several governments say the funding let Beijing discourage teaching on subjects it dislikes. Many US and European universities closed their institutes after 2019.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report (Feb 2019); Politico (2019); Hanban/CIEF announcements (July 2020)

n: Liaison Bureau, Political Work Department of the Central Military Commission (PLA)

how.caifc: CAIFC is a united front body subordinate to this Liaison Bureau, according to Project 2049 and the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.

d: The Liaison Bureau of the People's Liberation Army's Political Work Department handles the army's political warfare and intelligence work aimed at foreigners and Taiwan. The China Association for International Friendly Contact, founded in Beijing in 1984, presents itself as a friendship society that hosts foreign politicians, retired officers and business people. Researchers at the Project 2049 Institute and the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission report that it is run by the Liaison Bureau, with further ties to the Ministry of State Security. The arrangement lets military intelligence meet and cultivate influential foreigners under a civilian name.
cite: Mark Stokes and Russell Hsiao, Project 2049 Institute (2013); US-China Economic and Security Review Commission staff report (2018); Anne-Marie Brady

n: China Development Bank and Chinese state support

how.huawei: Raised Huawei's credit line from $10 billion in 2004 to $30 billion in 2009; the Wall Street Journal counted about $46 billion in state loans and $25 billion in tax cuts.

d: China Development Bank is a state policy bank that lends for the government's industrial goals. It gave Huawei a credit line of $10 billion in 2004, raised to $30 billion in 2009, which Huawei's customers could draw on to buy its equipment. The Wall Street Journal in 2019 counted roughly $46 billion in loans and other support and $25 billion in tax cuts from the Chinese state. In 2010 the EU trade commissioner said state support let Huawei underbid rivals by up to 70 per cent. Cheap state money helped Huawei win contracts for national telecom networks abroad. Huawei disputes the figures.
cite: Wall Street Journal (25 Dec 2019); EU Trade Commissioner Karel De Gucht (2010); China Development Bank announcements

n: State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC)

how.sinochem: Sinochem is a key central state-owned enterprise supervised by SASAC, an institution directly under the State Council.
how.powerchina: Wholly owns PowerChina, Sinohydro's parent, as a central state enterprise.
how.china_harbour: Owns China Communications Construction Company, CHEC's parent, as a central state enterprise.
how.zte: Its aerospace groups own the state shareholders of ZTE Holdings, ZTE's largest shareholder, and nominate 5 of its 9 directors.

d: SASAC is the Chinese government body that owns and supervises the largest state companies on behalf of the State Council. Sinochem, which merged with ChemChina and through it owns the Swiss seed and pesticide maker Syngenta, is one of the central firms under its supervision. SASAC appoints or approves senior managers and sets goals for these firms, so their purchases abroad and their lobbying serve state policy as well as profit. Its role is set out in Chinese law and in the companies' own filings.
cite: SASAC official descriptions; Sinochem and Syngenta Group filings; SASAC list of central state-owned enterprises; ZTE annual reports (2019)

n: Iranian state under the Supreme Leader

how.irgc_qf: The IRGC commander, over the Quds Force, is appointed by and reports to the Supreme Leader.
how.irgc_economic: The IRGC's business arm Khatam al-Anbiya, one of Iran's largest contractors, sits under the same chain of command.
how.hezbollah: Iran founded Hezbollah with about 1,500 Revolutionary Guards in 1982 and, by US estimates in 2018, gave it about $700 million a year.
how.hamas: Iran supplied money and weapons to Hamas, rising to about $150 million in 2012 before cuts over the Syrian war; the US sanctioned Bank Saderat for passing funds to it.
how.houthis: The IRGC Quds Force trained Houthi fighters and shipped them missiles, drones and rifles; UN experts found Iranian help behind Houthi ballistic missiles and UAVs.
how.sadrists: The Quds Force funded, trained and armed 'Special Groups' that split from the Mahdi Army, paying an estimated $750,000 to $3 million a month, US commanders said.

d: Iran's Supreme Leader, a post held by Ayatollah Ali Khamenei from 1989, commands the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. He appoints its commander, who answers to him. Under that command sit the Quds Force, which runs allied militias abroad, and a business empire led by the Khatam al-Anbiya construction headquarters, with more than 100 companies. The Iranian state also created Hezbollah in Lebanon in 1982, sending about 1,500 Guards to train it, and US officials estimated in 2018 that it was paying Hezbollah about $700 million a year. This lets Iran place armed and political allies inside other countries' parliaments and security forces.
cite: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran; US officials' estimates (2018); Los Angeles Times on IRGC business; academic histories of Hezbollah; US Treasury designation of Bank Saderat (2006); UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reports (2018, 2023); US military briefings (Gen. Kevin Bergner, 2007-08)

n: Chinyong IT Cooperation Company (DPRK Ministry of People's Armed Forces)

how.dprk_it_workers: The US Treasury said in March 2024 that Chinyong, tied to the Ministry of People's Armed Forces, sends IT worker teams abroad; its Russian arm paid it over $2.5 million in 2021-22.

d: North Korea sends thousands of IT workers abroad, or has them work remotely under false identities, to earn money for the state. The US Treasury said in March 2024 that Chinyong Information Technology Cooperation Company, linked to the Ministry of People's Armed Forces, manages these teams through front firms in Russia and the UAE. Its Russian subsidiary alone paid it more than $2.5 million in 2021-2022, and the Treasury says the money ends up funding weapons of mass destruction. The workers get hired inside foreign companies, giving the regime money and sometimes access to their systems.
cite: US Treasury press release JY2215 (27 Mar 2024)

n: Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA, now NIS)

how.unification: The 1978 Fraser report found that KCIA founder Kim Jong-pil organised the Unification Church in the early 1960s as a political tool and that the KCIA worked with Sun Myung Moon.
how.heritage_foundation: Heritage reportedly received $2.2 million from the South Korean intelligence agency in the 1980s.

d: The KCIA was South Korea's intelligence agency, founded in 1961 by Kim Jong-pil for the military ruler Park Chung Hee; it is now the National Intelligence Service. A US House investigation led by Donald Fraser reported in 1978 that the KCIA bribed members of Congress through Tongsun Park, planned to place a spy network in the White House, and worked with Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church, which Kim Jong-pil had organised as a political tool. Church members volunteered in congressional offices. The Heritage Foundation was later reported to have taken $2.2 million from the agency in the 1980s.
cite: US House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations' (Fraser report, 31 Oct 1978); reporting on Heritage funding

n: Republic of China (Taiwan) government and Kuomintang

how.wacl: Chiang Kai-shek initiated its forerunner, the Asian People's Anti-Communist League, in 1954; Taiwan's Foreign Ministry still funded the league, with a budget of NT$22 million in 2017.
how.blue_shirts: Chiang Kai-shek, leader of the Kuomintang and of the Republic of China, founded the Blue Shirts Society in 1932 and led it.

d: The Republic of China government on Taiwan, ruled for decades by Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang party, created the anti-communist league network. In 1954 Chiang, with the leaders of South Korea and the Philippines, set up the Asian People's Anti-Communist League, which grew in 1966 into the World Anti-Communist League with headquarters in Taipei. The league brought together governments, exiles and far-right movements on several continents during the Cold War. Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has continued to fund its successor, the World League for Freedom and Democracy, and its budget was debated in Taiwan's parliament in 2016-2017.
cite: WLFD history; Taipei Times (2016, 2017) on league budget; Frederic Wakeman, Spymaster: Dai Li and the Chinese Secret Service (2003); Maria Hsia Chang, The Chinese Blue Shirt Society (1985)

n: NATO Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) - Clandestine Planning Committee

how.gladio: The Clandestine Planning Committee was set up under the Supreme Allied Commander Europe around 1951-52 to coordinate national stay-behind networks; the European Parliament condemned US personnel at SHAPE for encouraging them.

d: SHAPE is NATO's military headquarters in Europe, now at Casteau near Mons in Belgium. Around 1951-52 an ad hoc Clandestine Planning Committee was set up under the Supreme Allied Commander to coordinate the secret 'stay-behind' networks that national spy services built to resist a Soviet invasion; an Allied Clandestine Committee followed in 1957. After Italian prime minister Giulio Andreotti admitted Gladio's existence in October 1990, the European Parliament passed a resolution on 22 November 1990 saying the networks were run by national services with NATO and protesting at the role of US military personnel at SHAPE.
cite: European Parliament resolution on Gladio (22 Nov 1990); Andreotti statement to the Italian Chamber of Deputies (24 Oct 1990); Belgian parliamentary inquiry (1991)

n: Nationalist Movement Party (MHP)

how.grey_wolves: Founded by MHP leader Alparslan Türkeş in the late 1960s as the party's youth and militant wing; led by MHP chairman Devlet Bahçeli since 1997.

d: The Nationalist Movement Party is a Turkish ultranationalist party, in alliance with President Erdoğan's AK Party since 2018. Its founder Alparslan Türkeş set up the Grey Wolves (Ülkü Ocakları) in the late 1960s as its youth and street-fighting wing; they were blamed for many killings in the political violence of 1976-1980. Since Türkeş died in 1997 the party's chairman, Devlet Bahçeli, has led both. A 1997 parliamentary inquiry after the Susurluk car crash, and documents in the Ergenekon trials, also pointed to ties between the Grey Wolves and state security officials. The party link is open and documented.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk inquiry report (April 1997); academic histories of the MHP

n: Abu Dhabi ruling family and United Arab Emirates state

how.bcci: Provided BCCI's start-up money in 1972, put in large deposits, and in April 1990 became its official 77 per cent owner.
how.interpol: Pledged €50 million to the Interpol Foundation in March 2017; its interior ministry general Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi was elected Interpol president in 2021.
how.cap: The UAE embassy gave the Center for American Progress between $500,000 and $999,999 in 2015.
how.rsf_sudan: Has been accused of arming the RSF through Chad; the UN Panel of Experts on Sudan called the allegations credible in January 2024, and the UAE denies them.
how.carlyle: Abu Dhabi's state fund Mubadala bought 7.5% of the Carlyle Group for $1.35 billion in September 2007.

d: The Al Nahyan family rules Abu Dhabi and leads the United Arab Emirates. Sheikh Zayed's government helped found BCCI in 1972 and became its official majority owner in 1990, a year before regulators shut the bank for fraud; a US Senate report found the family's stakes looked more like a nominee arrangement than true ownership. In 2017 the UAE pledged €50 million to the Interpol Foundation, and in 2021 a UAE police general became Interpol's president despite complaints about torture. The UAE embassy also funded the Center for American Progress. These gifts and stakes bought standing inside banks, police bodies and think tanks.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report, 1992); Interpol press release (27 Mar 2017); Center for American Progress donor list (2015); UN Panel of Experts on Sudan, final report S/2024/65 (Jan 2024); Carlyle Group press release on Mubadala investment (Sept 2007)

n: State of Qatar

how.fight_impunity: Eva Kaili's partner Francesco Giorgi testified that Qatar paid cash to Antonio Panzeri from 2019 and that bribes went through Fight Impunity; Qatar denies it.
how.glencore: Qatar's state fund holds about 8.2 per cent of Glencore through Qatar Holding LLC.
how.muslim_brotherhood: Hosted the Brotherhood's spiritual leader Yusuf al-Qaradawi from 1961 and gave him a show on state-funded Al Jazeera for about 20 years; it also sent money to Egypt under Brotherhood president Morsi. Qatar denies funding the group (probable).
how.hamas: Has hosted Hamas's political bureau in Doha since 2012 and sent hundreds of millions of dollars into Gaza, passed through Israel with the Netanyahu government's approval from 2018.

d: Qatar is a small, gas-rich Gulf monarchy whose state fund invests worldwide. Belgian prosecutors charged in December 2022 that Qatar paid European Parliament members and staff to speak well of it before the football World Cup; police found about €1.5 million in cash. Former MEP Antonio Panzeri, who ran the charity Fight Impunity, admitted guilt in a plea deal, and Francesco Giorgi said bribes were routed through the charity. Qatar denies wrongdoing and no trial date had been set by April 2026. Separately, Qatar Holding, part of the Qatar Investment Authority, is one of Glencore's two largest shareholders.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor (Dec 2022); Panzeri plea agreement (Jan 2023); Glencore shareholder register; Wikipedia, Muslim Brotherhood; CNN interview with Qatar's foreign minister (Dec 2019); New York Times, 'Buying Quiet: Inside the Israeli Plan That Propped Up Hamas' (10 Dec 2023); Reuters reporting on Qatari payments (2018-2023)

n: Moroccan government and foreign intelligence (DGED)

how.fight_impunity: Panzeri said the first cash came from Morocco, and an arrangement with Moroccan intelligence reportedly paid Panzeri and Giorgi €50,000 each a year.

d: Morocco's foreign intelligence agency, the DGED, is accused of paying members of the European Parliament to support Morocco's positions, such as on Western Sahara. In the 'Qatargate' case Antonio Panzeri, who founded the Brussels charity Fight Impunity, told investigators that Moroccan cash came first, before Qatar's. Francesco Giorgi confessed to receiving money from the Moroccan government, and reports describe a deal paying the two men €50,000 a year each. Morocco denies involvement. Panzeri pleaded guilty in January 2023, and the case was still awaiting trial in 2026.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor (2022-23); Panzeri and Giorgi statements reported by Le Soir, La Repubblica and Politico Europe

n: Aliyev family and Azerbaijan's ruling elite

how.caviar_lobby: Ran a $2.9 billion slush fund through Danske Bank Estonia in 2012-2014, nearly half from a shell company linked to the Aliyev family; some went to European politicians.

d: Azerbaijan has been ruled by Heydar Aliyev and then his son Ilham Aliyev since 1993. Between 2012 and 2014 its ruling elite moved about $2.9 billion through four British shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch. About $1.45 billion came from an account linked to the Aliyev family; some of the money paid European politicians and lobbyists to praise the government and play down repression. Italian MP Luca Volontè, who led a group in the Council of Europe's assembly, was jailed for four years for bribery in 2021. The scheme was exposed in 2017 by OCCRP and partner newspapers.
cite: OCCRP, 'The Azerbaijani Laundromat' (4 Sep 2017); PACE Independent Investigation Body report (April 2018); Milan court verdict on Volontè (Jan 2021)

n: Sackler family (Raymond and Mortimer Sackler branches)

how.purdue: Owned Purdue Pharma from 1952, sat on its board, and withdrew about $10.7 billion from it as legal pressure grew, according to a 2019 audit.

d: The Sacklers are the American family that owned Purdue Pharma, the maker of the painkiller OxyContin. Brothers Arthur, Raymond and Mortimer bought the firm in 1952, and all its profits went to family trusts. Richard Sackler ran its research and marketing as OxyContin was sold as low-risk. Eight family members had served on the board by 2018. An audit for the bankruptcy found the family took out $10.7 billion after the company came under legal scrutiny. Purdue pleaded guilty to federal crimes in 2007 and 2020 and was ordered to dissolve in 2026.
cite: AlixPartners audit (Dec 2019); US Department of Justice plea agreements (2007, 2020); Harrington v. Purdue Pharma (US Supreme Court, 2024)

n: Odebrecht family

how.odebrecht: Norberto Odebrecht founded the company in 1944; his grandson Marcelo, chief executive, was sentenced in 2016 to 19 years for bribing Petrobras executives.

d: The Odebrecht family founded and long controlled the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht, now called Novonor. Under chief executive Marcelo Odebrecht the company paid about $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries from 2001 to 2016. Marcelo was arrested in 2015 and sentenced in 2016 to 19 years and four months; the company paid a record $2.6 billion penalty in the United States. Former presidents in several countries were caught up in the case. Marcelo agreed to leave as a shareholder in 2022, and a family member still chairs the board.
cite: US Department of Justice plea agreement (21 Dec 2016); Brazilian federal court, Operation Car Wash (March 2016)

n: Iskandar and Akram Safa (owners of Privinvest)

how.privinvest: The Safa brothers owned Privinvest Holding; in 2024 London's High Court ordered Iskandar Safa's estate and Privinvest to pay about $1.9 billion to Mozambique over the 'tuna bond' bribes.

d: Iskandar Safa and his brother Akram owned Privinvest, a shipbuilding group based in Abu Dhabi. Privinvest sold boats and equipment to Mozambican state companies that were paid for with secret, state-guaranteed loans, the so-called 'tuna bonds', and Mozambique accused it of bribing officials to win the deals. Iskandar Safa died in January 2024; in July 2024 London's High Court found Privinvest liable and ordered his estate and the group to pay Mozambique about $1.9 billion.
cite: Republic of Mozambique v Credit Suisse and others, High Court of England and Wales, judgment of Mr Justice Robin Knowles (July 2024)

n: Gennady Timchenko

how.gunvor: Co-founded Gunvor with Torbjörn Törnqvist and held 43.5 per cent until March 2014; the US Treasury then alleged Putin had investments in Gunvor, which the company denies.

d: Gennady Timchenko is a Russian billionaire and long-time associate of Vladimir Putin from St Petersburg. With the Swede Torbjörn Törnqvist he built Gunvor, which became one of the largest traders of Russian oil. In March 2014, days before the US sanctioned him over Crimea, he sold his 43.5 per cent stake to Törnqvist. The US Treasury said at the time that Putin had investments in Gunvor and might have access to its funds; Gunvor denied it and no evidence was published. Gunvor later paid about $660 million in 2024 to settle US and Swiss cases over bribes in Ecuador.
cite: US Treasury press release (20 Mar 2014); Gunvor statements; US Department of Justice (March 2024)

n: Cambodian ruling elite (Hun Sen government and Cambodian People's Party)

how.prince_group: Chen Zhi served as an adviser to Hun Sen and to the Interior Ministry from 2017; Sar Sokha, later deputy prime minister, co-founded a casino with him in 2017.

d: Cambodia's People's Party has ruled since 1979, led by Hun Sen and since 2023 by his son Hun Manet. Chen Zhi, the founder of Prince Group, was made an adviser to Hun Sen, to senior ministers and to the Interior Ministry, which oversees the police. Sar Sokha, later deputy prime minister, co-founded a casino with him. In October 2025 the US charged Chen with running forced-labour scam compounds and seized about 127,271 bitcoin; the US and UK sanctioned the group. Cambodia arrested him and sent him to China in January 2026. The posts show official protection; how much leaders knew is not proven.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment (14 Oct 2025); US Treasury and UK FCDO sanctions (Oct 2025); Radio Free Asia and ICIJ reporting

n: Religious Technology Center (David Miscavige)

how.scientology: Controls the trademarks and texts of Scientology and licenses them to the church; David Miscavige, its board chairman since 1987, is the movement's leader.

d: The Religious Technology Center was set up by the Church of Scientology in 1982 to control the use of its trademarks and scriptures. It licenses them to the Church of Scientology International and earns fees, so it decides who may practise Scientology under that name. Its chairman since 1987, David Miscavige, is the movement's leader in practice. This structure puts the whole worldwide church, including its campaigns to win over officials and its lawsuits against critics, under one man's control. It is described in the church's own filings and US court cases.
cite: Religious Technology Center filings; US court records (e.g. RTC v. Netcom)

n: Warren Buffett

how.gates_foundation: Pledged about 10 million Berkshire Hathaway shares in 2006, the first gift worth about $1.5 billion, and was a trustee until 2021.

d: Warren Buffett is the head of the investment company Berkshire Hathaway. In 2006 he pledged most of his fortune, about 10 million Berkshire shares paid in yearly instalments, to the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and he served as a trustee until 2021. His gifts more than doubled the foundation's spending power. The foundation became the World Health Organization's second-largest funder, around 12 per cent of its budget, and a major voice in global health policy. Buffett said in 2024 that it will get no more of his money after his death.
cite: Buffett pledge letter (June 2006); Gates Foundation annual reports; WHO funding data

n: ExxonMobil

how.atlas_network: Gave Atlas Network about $1.08 million from 1998, according to ExxonSecrets.
how.alec: Was an ALEC member and funder until it left in 2018.
how.heritage_foundation: Is among the oil companies that funded Heritage while it questioned climate science.

d: ExxonMobil is the largest US oil company. For years it funded think tanks and lobby groups that cast doubt on climate science and opposed rules on emissions. It gave the Atlas Network of free-market think tanks about $1.08 million from 1998, paid to be a member of ALEC, where company lobbyists and state legislators write model bills, until it left in 2018, and funded the Heritage Foundation. These payments helped those groups push policies that suited the oil industry inside legislatures. The grants are recorded in Exxon's own giving reports and the ExxonSecrets database.
cite: ExxonMobil Worldwide Giving reports; Greenpeace ExxonSecrets; Union of Concerned Scientists (July 2018)

n: John Templeton Foundation

how.atlas_network: Is Atlas Network's largest listed grant-maker, about $9.67 million according to tax filings compiled by DeSmog.

d: The John Templeton Foundation was set up by the investor John Templeton and funds research on religion, science and free-market economics. According to tax filings compiled by DeSmog and Conservative Transparency, it has given the Atlas Network about $9.67 million, more than any other listed foundation. Atlas uses such money to help start and train free-market think tanks in many countries, which then lobby for tax cuts, privatisation and deregulation and send people into government posts. The figures come from the foundations' annual tax returns.
cite: DeSmog Atlas Network recipient table; IRS 990 filings; Conservative Transparency

n: DonorsTrust

how.atlas_network: Gave Atlas Network about $3 million, according to tax filings.
how.heritage_foundation: Listed Heritage among its grantees as of 2013.

d: DonorsTrust is a donor-advised fund in Virginia that lets wealthy donors give to conservative and free-market groups without their names appearing on the groups' records. It passed about $3 million to the Atlas Network and has made grants to the Heritage Foundation. Because the money goes through DonorsTrust, the public sees only its name, not the original donors. Its grants show up in its annual IRS filings.
cite: DonorsTrust IRS 990 filings; DeSmog; The Guardian (Feb 2013)

n: Andrej Babiš (via two trust funds)

how.agrofert: Babiš founded Agrofert and is the sole beneficiary of two trust funds that own all of its shares, according to the Slovak beneficial-ownership register.

d: Andrej Babiš is the Czech billionaire who founded the agriculture, food and chemicals group Agrofert and later became prime minister. In 2017 he put his shares into two trust funds, but the Slovak public register of beneficial owners lists him as the sole beneficiary of both funds, which own all of Agrofert. A European Commission audit, final in 2021, found him in a conflict of interest, because as head of government he helped set and manage the EU subsidies that his own company received. Transparency International Czech Republic first raised the issue in 2018.
cite: Transparency International press release (Dec 2019); Radio Prague International reports on final EU audit (2021)

n: Presidency of Azerbaijan (Ilham Aliyev)

how.socar: SOCAR is fully state-owned and its president is appointed by decree of the president of Azerbaijan, as Ilham Aliyev did in July 2022.
how.electrogas: Through its trading arm, state-owned SOCAR holds a share of Electrogas Malta alongside Siemens and the local GEM Holdings group, and supplied the gas under the deal.

d: Azerbaijan's president controls the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR). The company is wholly owned by the state, and the president names its head by decree. SOCAR is described as a main source of income for the government and runs opaque contracts through middlemen. Through SOCAR Trading it is also one of three equal owners of Electrogas Malta, the gas power-station consortium at the centre of the 17 Black bribery and Daphne Caruana Galizia murder inquiries, and it was the gas supplier under that deal. This gives the Azerbaijani state a direct stake in a Maltese state contract.
cite: SOCAR founding and appointment decrees; Lovin Malta on Electrogas ownership (2020); The Shift News Electrogas ownership report (2020)

n: Yorgen Fenech and the Tumas Group (Fenech family)

how.seventeen_black: Fenech admitted owning 17 Black, the Dubai-registered company named in leaked documents as a planned source of payments to Keith Schembri and Konrad Mizzi.
how.electrogas: Fenech was a director and beneficial owner of Electrogas; Tumas Energy holds about 35% of GEM Holdings, one of the three equal owners, and he personally held about 8% through New Energy Ltd.

d: Yorgen Fenech ran the Tumas Group, a Maltese family business that owns the Hilton in Malta, and holds its controlling share. He was a director and part-owner of Electrogas, which won the state contract to build and supply a gas power station. He also secretly owned 17 Black, a company in Dubai. A Panama Papers email suggested that two of the prime minister's closest aides, Keith Schembri and Konrad Mizzi, were to receive up to US$2 million from 17 Black. Police named Fenech as its owner in 2018 and Reuters and the Times of Malta made this public. He was charged in 2019 over Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder and acquitted in 2026.
cite: Reuters and Times of Malta (Nov 2018); Lovin Malta (2020); public inquiry into the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia

n: Shaul Elovitch and Eurocom (Elovitch family)

how.bezeq: Eurocom, owned by Elovitch and his family, was Bezeq's controlling shareholder through its subsidiary B Communications from 2010, and Elovitch chaired Bezeq.

d: Shaul Elovitch built the Eurocom holding group and in 2010 took control of Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, through a Eurocom subsidiary. He chaired Bezeq, and his son sat on its board. Bezeq owned the news site Walla!. In December 2020 Elovitch, his son and three others were indicted on fraud, breach of trust and securities charges, and his wife Iris on bribery. Prosecutors say Walla! gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu favourable coverage while his ministry gave Bezeq regulatory help worth large sums. The case (Case 4000) grew out of a Securities Authority inquiry into Bezeq's 2015 purchase of Yes from Eurocom.
cite: Calcalist Tech (Feb 2018); Times of Israel; indictment reporting (Dec 2020)

n: Wallenberg Foundations (Foundation Asset Management)

how.wallenberg: The Wallenberg foundations control 50% of the votes in Investor AB, the holding company created in 1916 to own the industrial shares of the family's Stockholms Enskilda Bank.
how.ericsson: Through Investor AB the foundations held 22.5% of the votes in Ericsson (2019), with a 7.2% capital stake, thanks to shares carrying extra votes.
how.abb: Through Investor AB the foundations held 11.8% of ABB's capital and votes (2019), making Investor its largest shareholder.

d: The Wallenberg foundations, led by the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, are charitable funds set up by the Swedish banking family. Together they control half the votes in Investor AB, which Jacob and Marcus Wallenberg chair. Investor in turn holds large blocks in companies such as ABB, Ericsson, SEB, Saab and AstraZeneca. In Ericsson, special shares with extra voting rights gave Investor 22.5% of the votes for only 7.2% of the capital. This chain lets one family steer the boards of many of Sweden's biggest companies while owning a small share of their capital. The figures are published by Investor AB.
cite: Patricia Industries / Investor AB ownership page; Investor AB annual figures (31 Dec 2019); Ericsson history of ownership control

n: French state (Agence des participations de l'État / SOGEPA)

how.airbus: The French state holds about 10.8% of Airbus through SOGEPA, as part of a shareholder partnership with Germany and Spain that together holds 25.7%.
how.thales: The French state holds about 26.6% of Thales and has a board member representing it, under a shareholder pact with Dassault Aviation.

d: The French state owns large stakes in its main defence and aerospace firms through the Agence des participations de l'État, a Finance Ministry agency, and its holding company SOGEPA. It holds about 10.8% of Airbus, as part of a partnership with the German and Spanish governments that together hold a quarter of the company. It holds about 26.6% of Thales, where it shares control with Dassault under a shareholders' pact and names a director. These stakes give the government a say over strategy, leadership and sales of companies that have been at the centre of foreign bribery cases. The holdings appear in company filings.
cite: Airbus shareholder structure (31 Dec 2024); MarketScreener Thales shareholders; Thales notice on French State board member

n: Dassault family (Groupe Industriel Marcel Dassault)

how.thales: The family's group owns Dassault Aviation, which holds about 26.6% of Thales, joint largest with the French state, and has sought an active role in choosing its leaders.

d: The Dassault family owns Groupe Industriel Marcel Dassault, the holding company founded on Marcel Dassault's aircraft business. Its main subsidiary, Dassault Aviation, makes the Rafale fighter. In 2008-2009 Dassault Aviation bought Alcatel-Lucent's stake in Thales and became, with the French state, one of the two main shareholders, with about 26.6%. Dassault said it would not be a passive partner, and board decisions such as the choice of chief executive have been fought out between the two. The family's wealth is estimated at about €23.5 billion. The stake is on public shareholder registers.
cite: AFP via WebManagerCenter (Dec 2008, May 2009); MarketScreener Thales shareholders

n: Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance (with Cassa Depositi e Prestiti)

how.eni: The state holds about 33.1% of Eni: 2.2% directly through the Ministry and 30.9% through Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, the state lender it controls.
how.leonardo: The Ministry of Economy and Finance is Leonardo's largest shareholder, with 30.2% (March 2025).

d: Italy's Ministry of Economy and Finance holds the controlling stakes in the country's oil company Eni and its defence group Leonardo (formerly Finmeccanica). In Eni it holds about a third of the shares, mostly through Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, a state-controlled lender. In Leonardo it holds about 30%. As the largest owner the government in practice chooses the chief executives and boards. Both companies have faced foreign bribery cases, including Eni in Nigeria and Algeria and AgustaWestland in India. The stakes are listed in public shareholder records.
cite: Eni and Leonardo shareholder records (2025-2026)

n: Saudi royal family and government

how.bae: After a Saudi threat to end counter-terrorism cooperation and drop a Typhoon order, the UK Serious Fraud Office halted its BAE bribery probe in December 2006; reports alleged BAE paid hundreds of millions of pounds to Prince Bandar bin Sultan.
how.isi: Saudi payments to Pakistan's army and ISI in the mid-1990s were undisclosed but probably reached several hundred million dollars in some years; Saudi money also flowed through ISI to the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s.
how.muslim_brotherhood: Gave refuge and teaching jobs to thousands of Egyptian Brothers fleeing Nasser from 1954 and helped fund the movement for over half a century, until relations broke and Riyadh listed it as terrorist in March 2014.

d: The Saudi ruling family has been the main customer behind the UK's largest arms deal, Al Yamamah, supplied by BAE Systems since the 1980s. Reports by the BBC and Guardian alleged that BAE paid hundreds of millions of pounds to Prince Bandar bin Sultan. In 2006 the head of the Serious Fraud Office said the Saudi side had threatened to end counter-terrorism cooperation, and the inquiry was dropped. The High Court called this unlawful in 2008; the House of Lords overturned that ruling. Saudi Arabia has also funded Pakistan's army and its intelligence service, ISI, which channelled US and Saudi money to Afghan fighters in the 1980s.
cite: The Corner House judicial review record; R (Corner House) v Director of the SFO [2008] UKHL 60; BBC Panorama (2007); US DOJ BAE plea (2010); Wikipedia, Muslim Brotherhood

n: Government of Abu Dhabi (Supreme Petroleum Council; Mohamed bin Zayed)

how.adnoc: ADNOC is owned by the Abu Dhabi government, is chaired by Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and is governed by the Supreme Petroleum Council acting as its board.

d: The Abu Dhabi government owns the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company outright. Its chairman is Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, ruler of Abu Dhabi and president of the UAE, and the Supreme Petroleum Council acts as its board. ADNOC's chief executive, Sultan Al Jaber, is also a UAE minister and was president of the COP28 climate summit in 2023. This means the same ruling family controls a large oil producer and, through its officials, has held the chair of the UN climate talks that set rules for fossil fuels.
cite: ADNOC corporate governance; COP28 presidency records

n: Trafigura (Swiss commodity trader)

how.sakunda: In 2013 Trafigura bought 49% of a joint venture with Sakunda that gained priority access to Zimbabwe's fuel pipeline; it paid Tagwirei at least US$100 million in fees and bought out his 51% in 2019.

d: Trafigura is one of the world's largest oil and metals traders. In 2013 it formed a joint venture with Kuda Tagwirei's Sakunda, taking 49%, after Sakunda had won rights over Zimbabwe's state fuel pipeline. The venture made at least US$1 billion in prepayments to the state pipeline company and controlled up to 80% of the country's fuel imports. OCCRP found that Tagwirei received at least US$100 million in fees, much of it sent offshore. Trafigura bought his share in 2019. Trafigura disputes OCCRP's figures, and Tagwirei denies wrongdoing.
cite: OCCRP investigation 'How a Zimbabwe Tycoon Made a Fortune from a Trafigura Partnership'

n: Emmerson Mnangagwa and ZANU-PF

how.sakunda: US Treasury says Tagwirei used his relationship with President Mnangagwa to win state contracts and hard currency, and that Mnangagwa's son handled the president's business interests linked to Tagwirei.

d: Emmerson Mnangagwa has been Zimbabwe's president since the 2017 coup and leads the ruling party ZANU-PF. The US Treasury, in sanctions decisions in 2020 and 2022, said Kuda Tagwirei used his relationship with Mnangagwa to obtain state contracts and scarce US dollars. It said Sakunda financed the Command Agriculture programme, which could not account for about US$3 billion, and that the president's son Emmerson Jr ran the president's business interests tied to Tagwirei. A ZANU-PF official said Tagwirei gave the party fuel, food and US$1.6 million around the 2017 coup. He later joined the party's Central Committee. Both men deny corruption.
cite: US Treasury press releases (5 Aug 2020; 12 Dec 2022 jy1158); VOA (2020)

n: VR Capital Group (hedge fund)

how.pid: VR Capital's Cayman fund bought 25% of P&ID after the 2017 arbitration win and directed its US$11 billion claim against Nigeria; in a 2021 filing it said P&ID's payments to Nigerian officials were unlawful.

d: VR Capital is an investment fund that buys distressed assets. After Process & Industrial Developments (P&ID) won an arbitration award against Nigeria in 2017, VR's Cayman Islands fund bought 25% of the company; Semafor reported it took control. It funded and directed the effort to enforce the award, which with interest grew to about US$11 billion. In a confidential 2021 filing it said P&ID's payments to two oil ministry officials were unlawful, while in the High Court it argued they were legal. In October 2023 the High Court in London set the award aside, finding it was obtained by fraud and bribery.
cite: BusinessDay Nigeria (2019); Semafor (20 Mar 2023); Nigeria v P&ID [2023] EWHC 2638 (Comm)

n: Joseph Kabila (former president of DR Congo)

how.gertler: US Treasury says Gertler used his close friendship with Kabila to act as middleman for mining sales, forcing some multinationals to go through him; Congo reportedly lost over US$1.36 billion in 2010-2012.

d: Joseph Kabila was president of the Democratic Republic of Congo from 2001 to 2019. The US Treasury sanctioned Dan Gertler in December 2017, saying he used his close friendship with Kabila to act as a go-between in the sale of mining assets. It said some multinational companies had to go through Gertler to deal with the Congolese state. Mining assets sold cheaply to offshore companies linked to him reportedly cost Congo more than US$1.36 billion between 2010 and 2012. Kabila had earlier named Gertler a special envoy. Gertler denies wrongdoing.
cite: US Treasury press releases (21 Dec 2017; 15 Jun 2018 sm0417)

n: Julio Ponce Lerou

how.sqm: Ponce Lerou is SQM's principal shareholder through a chain of holding companies (the 'cascades'); SQM admitted to US authorities that about US$14.75 million went to Chilean politically exposed persons in 2008-2015.

d: Julio Ponce Lerou is a former son-in-law of the dictator Augusto Pinochet and ran state forestry companies under the military government. He became the main shareholder of SQM, the Chilean lithium and fertiliser company that was privatised under Pinochet, holding it through a chain of companies known as the 'cascades'. In 2017 SQM settled with the US SEC and Justice Department for US$30 million, admitting that about US$14.75 million was paid from a discretionary fund to Chilean politicians and their aides through fake invoices. Ponce was not charged in that case but faced the separate 'Cascadas' fraud case over the holding companies.
cite: SEC order In re SQM (Release 79795, Jan 2017); US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement; CIPER Chile

n: Joesley and Wesley Batista (J&F Investimentos)

how.jbs: The brothers wholly own J&F Investimentos, which controls JBS with about 42%; in 2017 J&F admitted giving about US$150 million, mostly bribes, to politicians and agreed US$3.2 billion in fines.

d: Joesley and Wesley Batista own J&F Investimentos, the family holding that controls JBS, the world's largest meat company. In a 2017 plea deal Joesley told prosecutors that J&F had paid bribes to many Brazilian politicians, and J&F agreed to pay about US$3.2 billion in fines. The company admitted giving roughly US$150 million, mostly in bribes, over about 25 years. Joesley also secretly recorded President Michel Temer. The money helped JBS win state loans, tax decisions and regulatory approvals. The politicians named denied taking bribes.
cite: J&F leniency agreement (May 2017); Brazilian Federal Prosecutors; Reuters

n: BNDES and BNDESPar (Brazilian Development Bank)

how.jbs: BNDES and its investment arm BNDESPar put about US$2.5 billion into JBS in 2007-2010 through loans and share and bond purchases, financing its global takeovers, and became a major minority shareholder.

d: BNDES is Brazil's state development bank, and BNDESPar is its investment arm. Between 2007 and 2010 it put about US$2.5 billion into JBS through loans and purchases of shares and bonds. This paid for JBS's purchases of US and other foreign meat firms and turned a regional company into a world leader. The financing was later examined in the corruption cases against the Batista brothers. In 2017 BNDESPar, as a large shareholder, called a meeting to try to remove the family from the board. The state bank's role shows how public money built a company that then paid politicians.
cite: Forbes Brasil (June 2017); BNDES statements; JBS filings

n: Agribusiness associations and multinationals funding Instituto Pensar Agro

how.pensar_agro: IPA is maintained by 48 trade associations whose members include Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, Cargill, Bunge, ADM, Louis Dreyfus, JBS, Marfrig, Nestlé and Danone; it writes the legislative agenda of Congress's farm caucus (FPA).

d: Instituto Pensar Agro is a lobby group in Brasília that drafts the legislative agenda and positions of the Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária, the farm caucus in Brazil's Congress. It is paid for by 48 trade associations. The research group De Olho nos Ruralistas traced these associations to multinational firms in pesticides and seeds (Bayer, BASF, Syngenta), grain trading (Cargill, Bunge, ADM, Louis Dreyfus), meat (JBS, Marfrig) and food (Nestlé, Danone). Between 2019 and 2022 these companies also held 278 meetings with Agriculture Ministry officials. This chain lets foreign and domestic companies shape farm and environmental law through the caucus.
cite: De Olho nos Ruralistas, 'Os Financiadores da Boiada' report (July 2022)

n: Mahmoud Karzai and Haseen Fahim (brothers of Afghanistan's president and first vice-president)

how.kabul_bank: Both were Kabul Bank shareholders and borrowers; Mahmoud Karzai was listed as owing US$22.2 million and Haseen Fahim US$4.4 million, and they escaped prosecution under a presidential decree for those who repaid.

d: Mahmoud Karzai is the brother of former president Hamid Karzai, and Abdul Haseen Fahim the brother of former first vice-president Mohammad Qasim Fahim. Both were shareholders of Kabul Bank, Afghanistan's largest private bank, which collapsed in 2010 after about US$935 million was stolen, mostly through fake loans to insiders. Afghan records list Karzai as still owing US$22.2 million and Fahim US$4.4 million. They were not prosecuted, because a decree by President Karzai gave immunity to those who returned money. The founder and chief executive were jailed. Their presence among the owners gave the bank political cover.
cite: RFE/RL (Oct 2014); Independent Joint Anti-Corruption Monitoring and Evaluation Committee report (2012)

n: Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), Iran

how.swedish_gangs: US Treasury says Foxtrot leader Rawa Majid cooperated with MOIS and that Foxtrot attacked the Israeli embassy in Stockholm for Iran in January 2024; Sweden's Säpo said Iran uses criminal networks in Sweden for violence.

d: Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security is the country's main civilian spy service. In May 2024 Sweden's Security Service said Iran was using Swedish criminal networks to carry out violence against Israeli and other targets. Israeli intelligence named the Foxtrot and Rumba gangs. In March 2025 the US Treasury sanctioned Foxtrot and its leader Rawa Majid, saying he cooperated with the Ministry and that the gang attacked the Israeli embassy in Stockholm for Iran in January 2024. Reports say Majid was arrested in Iran and told to cooperate. This lets Tehran use gang members, often teenagers, as hired proxies abroad.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0047 (12 Mar 2025); Säpo statement (30 May 2024); VOA

n: Iranian Foreign Ministry and its Institute for Political and International Studies (IPIS)

how.iran_experts_initiative: Emails show the initiative was started in 2014 and managed by Foreign Ministry diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh and IPIS head Mostafa Zahrani to promote Iran's nuclear position through Western academics.

d: Iran's Foreign Ministry runs a think tank, the Institute for Political and International Studies. Emails obtained by Semafor and Iran International show that in spring 2014 the ministry's diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh and IPIS head Mostafa Zahrani set up the Iran Experts Initiative. It gathered a core group of academics in the West to place opinion pieces and analysis supporting a nuclear deal, and some members later held advisory posts in Western governments and think tanks. The International Crisis Group and one participant dispute that it was government-directed, calling it an informal platform.
cite: Semafor and Iran International joint investigation (25 Sep 2023)

n: Chinese Communist Party (Taiwan Affairs Office and related bodies)

how.cupp_bamboo: Taiwanese prosecutors in 2024 charged a CUPP couple with taking about NT$74 million from the CCP for propaganda and election interference; a 2018 probe examined money from Chinese officials and state firms laundered into the party.

d: The Chinese Communist Party runs work aimed at Taiwan through the Taiwan Affairs Office and United Front bodies. The Chinese Unification Promotion Party was founded by Chang An-lo, a former leader of the Bamboo Union gang, while he lived in China. In 2018 Taiwanese investigators looked into money from Chinese officials and state-linked companies reaching the party. In November 2024 prosecutors charged CUPP members Chang Meng-chung and Hung Wen-ting with taking about NT$74 million (US$2.3 million) from the CCP for propaganda and to sway elections. The interior ministry then asked the Constitutional Court to dissolve the party. Chang denies the money comes from any government.
cite: Taipei Times (8 Aug 2018; 7 Nov 2024); Gulf Times/AFP (2018)

n: Myanmar military (Tatmadaw) and its party, the USDP

how.karen_bgf: In 2010 Saw Chit Thu's force became a Border Guard Force under Tatmadaw command and took military money and supplies until January 2024; US Treasury says it still cooperated with the military in September 2024.
how.kokang_families: In 2009 the military helped Bai Suocheng oust the Kokang leader, then put his men into Border Guard Force 1006 and made him head of the Kokang zone; Bai, Ming and Liu family members sat as MPs for the military-backed USDP.
how.ma_ba_tha: In June 2019 military spokesman Brigadier General Zaw Min Tun gave 30 million kyats to Ma Ba Tha's successor body, the Buddha Dhamma Parahita Foundation, after it protested the case against Wirathu (probable backing; relations later mixed).

d: Myanmar's armed forces built alliances with border militias by turning them into Border Guard Forces under army command. In 2010 Saw Chit Thu's Karen militia joined this scheme and received money and supplies; his base at Shwe Kokko grew into a scam and trafficking hub. In 2009 the army helped Bai Suocheng seize Kokang, then made him head of the self-administered zone. Bai, Ming Xuechang and Liu Zhangqi became MPs for the army's party, the USDP. China later issued warrants for these families over scam centres, and a Chinese court sentenced Bai to death in 2025. Protection by the army let these groups run casinos and scam compounds.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0129 (5 May 2025); RFA (Dec 2023); Shenzhen court verdict (Nov 2025); Wikipedia, Ma Ba Tha (citing Myanmar press, 2019)

n: Government of Laos (Lao People's Revolutionary Party)

how.zhao_wei_tco: In 2007 the Lao government set up the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone with Kings Romans and granted it a 99-year lease over 10,000 hectares, under which Zhao Wei's group runs the zone.

d: The Lao government, run by its single ruling party, created the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in 2007 together with Kings Romans Group, owned by Zhao Wei and his wife. It granted the company a 99-year lease over 10,000 hectares on the Mekong, 3,000 of them a duty-free zone. In 2018 the US Treasury sanctioned Zhao Wei's network for drug, wildlife and human trafficking and money laundering through the casino. The Diplomat describes the zone as under the de facto rule of Zhao's company, helped by ties to the Lao elite. Lao authorities have made some raids since. Zhao denies the charges.
cite: US Treasury sanctions (30 Jan 2018); The Diplomat (Apr 2021); RFA (Nov 2022)

n: Indonesian Army and its party IPKI (General A. H. Nasution); later Golkar

how.pemuda_pancasila: Pemuda Pancasila was founded in 1959 as the youth wing of IPKI, a party General Nasution set up to advance the army's political interests; it later sat inside Golkar, Suharto's ruling vehicle, from 1982 to 2001.

d: Pemuda Pancasila began in 1959 as the youth wing of IPKI, a party that General Abdul Haris Nasution created to push the Indonesian Army's political aims. In 1965-66, after the failed coup, its members took part in the killings of suspected communists, especially in Medan, and seized communist property in Jakarta. Under Suharto's New Order it backed the regime and from 1982 to 2001 was part of Golkar, the government's political vehicle. Its army origins gave it protection and a role as a civilian enforcer.
cite: Pancasila Youth history (Antara; CNN Indonesia, 2025); academic studies of the 1965-66 killings

n: Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP)

how.peoples_aman_committee: The Lyari gang's Aman Committee backed the PPP, which ruled 2008-2013; senior PPP leader Zulfiqar Mirza said in March 2011 that the committee was the PPP's wing.

d: The Pakistan Peoples Party ruled Pakistan from 2008 to 2013 and Sindh province for longer. The Peoples' Aman Committee was set up in Karachi's Lyari district in 2008 by gang leader Rehman Dakait and later led by his cousin Uzair Baloch. It supported the PPP, and in March 2011 Zulfiqar Mirza, then Sindh home minister and a senior PPP figure, publicly called it the PPP's wing; he later described it as a social group. Under pressure from the MQM, its allies, the PPP distanced itself, and the committee was banned in October 2011 under the anti-terrorism law.
cite: Samaa TV (6 Mar 2011); Daily Times; Pakistan government ban notice (Oct 2011)

n: Government of El Salvador under Nayib Bukele

how.ms13: US Treasury said in December 2021 that officials Osiris Luna and Carlos Marroquín secretly negotiated with MS-13 and Barrio 18 leaders and gave them financial incentives and prison privileges in 2020 in exchange for fewer killings and electoral support.

d: Nayib Bukele has been president of El Salvador since 2019. In September 2020 the newspaper El Faro reported secret talks between his officials and the jailed leaders of MS-13. In December 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned the prisons chief Osiris Luna and Carlos Marroquín, head of a government social programme. It said they negotiated with gang leaders, gave MS-13 and Barrio 18 financial incentives and privileges such as phones in prison, and sought gang support for Bukele's party before the 2021 elections. US prosecutors also said gang leaders were released. Bukele calls the accusations absurd, and since 2022 his government has jailed tens of thousands of suspected gang members.
cite: US Treasury sanctions (8 Dec 2021); El Faro (Sep 2020); InSight Crime

n: Michel Martelly (former president of Haiti)

how.viv_ansanm: US Treasury said in August 2024 that Martelly sponsored multiple Haitian gangs and laundered drug money; the gangs were not named in the reporting confirmed here, so the link to the Viv Ansanm alliance specifically is not proven.

d: Michel Martelly was president of Haiti from 2011 to 2016. In August 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him, saying he had abused his influence to help move drugs, worked with Haitian drug traffickers, helped launder drug money and sponsored multiple gangs. Gangs that later joined the Viv Ansanm alliance now control most of Port-au-Prince. Canada has separately sanctioned business leaders, including Gilbert Bigio, Reynold Deeb and Sherif Abdallah, for protecting and enabling gangs. Martelly denies the accusations. This record shows that a former head of state stood behind gangs, but not which ones.
