cite: US Treasury sanctions (20 Aug 2024); Al Jazeera; CTV News on Canadian sanctions

n: Viktor Medvedchuk

how.voice_of_europe: Czech intelligence found Medvedchuk and his associate Artem Marchevskyi ran Voice of Europe from Prague and paid pro-Russian politicians; Marchevskyi worked closely with an FSB unit; Czech and EU sanctions followed in 2024.

d: Viktor Medvedchuk is a former Ukrainian politician and close associate of Vladimir Putin, who has lived in Russia since a prisoner exchange in 2022. In March 2024 the Czech government said its security service had found that he and his associate Artem Marchevskyi ran the Prague-based website Voice of Europe as a Russian influence operation. The network allegedly paid far-right politicians in at least five EU countries, and reports put the sums at up to €1 million a month. Marchevskyi was said to work with an FSB unit. The Czech Republic and then the EU, in May 2024, sanctioned both men and the outlet.
cite: Czech Foreign Ministry and BIS statements (Mar 2024); EU Council sanctions (27 May 2024); Kyiv Independent

n: Korean Central Intelligence Agency under President Park Chung-hee

how.koreagate: Tongsun Park was indicted in 1977 for, among other things, failing to register as a KCIA agent, and was charged with bribing US Congress members with South Korean government money; a former KCIA director testified to his role.

d: In the 1970s South Korea's military-led government under Park Chung-hee feared the United States would withdraw its troops. Its intelligence agency, the KCIA, ran an effort to win over the US Congress. The businessman Tongsun Park was charged with bribing members of Congress with South Korean government money and was indicted in 1977 on 36 counts, including failing to register as a KCIA agent. Former KCIA director Kim Hyong-uk testified about the scheme. Park admitted giving cash to about 30 members. One congressman was convicted and others were reprimanded. The scandal is known as Koreagate.
cite: US House Ethics Committee investigation (1977-78); Tongsun Park indictment (1977); Time (Nov 1976)

n: Jacques Foccart and the Gaullist leadership

how.sac_fr: Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, co-founded the SAC in 1960 with Pierre Debizet and was its real leader; it reported to de Gaulle through him and its local chiefs sat on Gaullist party committees.

d: Jacques Foccart was Charles de Gaulle's adviser on African affairs and intelligence. In January 1960 he and Pierre Debizet created the Service d'Action Civique, a Gaullist militia. Foccart was its real leader, and it reported to de Gaulle through him. Its regional heads were members of the Gaullist party's local committees, and it recruited from the movement and from organised crime. It was used against the OAS, organised the May 1968 counter-demonstration, and was suspected in covert actions. After the 1981 Auriol massacre involving its members, the Mitterrand government dissolved it in 1982.
cite: French parliamentary commission of inquiry into the SAC (1982); dissolution decree (3 Aug 1982)

n: Swedish Social Democratic Party (SAP) leadership

how.ib_sweden: IB director Birger Elmér reported regularly to Social Democratic party secretary and defence minister Sven Andersson and had contact with Olof Palme, according to former security chief P. G. Vinge; Palme denied any link.

d: The Social Democrats governed Sweden for most of the 20th century. Informationsbyrån (IB) was a secret intelligence unit that, as journalists revealed in 1973, also spied on left-wing Swedes. Its director Birger Elmér reported to senior ministers, most likely defence minister Sven Andersson, who was also the party's secretary, and Prime Minister Olof Palme. Former security police chief P. G. Vinge wrote that Elmér had regular contact with both. Palme denied a link, and the journalists who exposed IB were jailed. A 2002 government inquiry examined the case in detail.
cite: Folket i Bild/Kulturfront (May 1973); SOU 2002:92 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten'

n: Bonanno crime family (New York)

how.montreal_mafia: In the 1970s the Bonanno family switched its support from Paolo Violi to Nicolo Rizzuto, helping the Rizzutos take over Montreal; the FBI still treats the Rizzuto organisation as a Bonanno faction.

d: The Bonanno family is one of New York's five Mafia families. Montreal's Mafia historically answered to it. In the 1970s, after wiretaps aired at a Quebec inquiry damaged the reputation of the Montreal boss Paolo Violi, the Bonannos moved their support to the Sicilian faction led by Nicolo Rizzuto. Violi and his brothers were killed and by the mid-1980s the Rizzutos ran Montreal's underworld, allied with the Cuntrera-Caruana clan. The FBI treats the Rizzuto family as a Bonanno faction, while Canadian agencies treat it as independent.
cite: Quebec Commission of Inquiry on Organized Crime (CECO, 1970s); FBI assessments

n: Gulf financiers on the 'Golden Chain' list

how.al_qaeda: A list seized in Sarajevo in 2002 named about 20 Saudi and Gulf financiers of bin Laden's early network; the 9/11 Commission said al-Qaeda relied on donors and charities, needing about US$30 million a year.

d: The 'Golden Chain' is a handwritten list seized in a 2002 raid on a charity in Sarajevo. It names about 20 wealthy Saudi and Gulf donors who funded the Afghan Arab fighters and Osama bin Laden's network in the late 1980s, with bin Laden's name appearing among the recipients. The 9/11 Commission found that al-Qaeda needed about US$30 million a year and raised most of it from donors in the Gulf and through charities, not from bin Laden's own wealth. A 2009 US cable said funding from Saudi Arabia remained a serious concern. The donors named have denied knowingly funding terrorism.
cite: 9/11 Commission Report and Monograph on Terrorist Financing (2004); US court filings citing the Golden Chain document

n: Taliban (Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan)

how.al_qaeda: After bin Laden left Sudan in 1996, the Taliban gave al-Qaeda a base in Afghanistan and refused to hand him over before and after 9/11.

d: The Taliban ruled most of Afghanistan from 1996 to 2001 and again since 2021, with their leader based in Kandahar. After Osama bin Laden left Sudan in 1996, they let al-Qaeda set up its headquarters and training camps in Afghanistan. They refused US demands to hand him over, which the United States cited when it invaded in 2001. UN monitoring reports since 2021 have said al-Qaeda figures remain in the country, and the group's leader Ayman al-Zawahiri was killed by a US strike in Kabul in 2022. The protection gave al-Qaeda safe ground to plan attacks.
cite: 9/11 Commission Report (2004); UN Security Council Monitoring Team reports

n: Pakistan Army (General Headquarters)

how.isi: ISI is headed by a serving army lieutenant-general chosen from names the army chief puts forward, and reports to both the army chief and the prime minister.

d: The Pakistan Army is the most powerful institution in Pakistan and has ruled the country directly for long periods. Its intelligence agency, Inter-Services Intelligence, is headed by a serving three-star army general. The army chief puts forward a short list of names and the prime minister picks one, and the head of ISI then reports to both. In the 1980s ISI was the main channel for US and Saudi money to Afghan fighters. The army's control means ISI serves the military's own aims, including in domestic politics, rather than only the elected government.
cite: Pakistani government and press accounts of DG ISI appointments; academic histories of Operation Cyclone

n: Kim Jong Un and the North Korean leadership

how.rgb_dprk: The Reconnaissance General Bureau reports directly to the top defence body and to Kim Jong Un as supreme commander; its IT-worker scheme sends earnings back to fund weapons programmes.

d: Kim Jong Un rules North Korea as head of the ruling Workers' Party, the state and the armed forces. The Reconnaissance General Bureau, the country's main foreign spy and covert operations agency, reports directly to the top defence body and to him as supreme commander. Its Department 53 runs schemes in which North Koreans use stolen identities to get remote jobs at foreign companies, each earning on average about US$300,000 a year, with the money sent home for weapons. UN reports also describe businesses it runs in Cambodia. These operations earn foreign currency for the government despite sanctions.
cite: UN Panel of Experts reports on DPRK; US Justice Department IT-worker indictments

n: KGB (Soviet Committee for State Security)

how.cuba_dgi: The KGB trained about 1,500 Cuban intelligence officers after 1962, and in 1970 a KGB team purged the directorate of officers it saw as anti-Soviet and had its chief replaced by a pro-Soviet officer.
how.stasi_hva: Soviet state-security advisers led by Andrei Grauer, later a KGB officer, attended the founding of the HVA's forerunner in 1951, and the HVA passed much of its intelligence to the KGB.
how.czech_intel: Soviet state-security advisers arrived in the StB in 1949 and reshaped it on Stalinist lines, purging older officers.

d: The KGB was the Soviet Union's security and foreign intelligence service, based at the Lubyanka in Moscow. After the 1962 missile crisis it trained about 1,500 officers of Cuba's intelligence directorate in Moscow. In 1970 a KGB team led by General Viktor Semyonov purged the Cuban service of officers it considered anti-Soviet; its chief, Manuel Piñeiro, was removed and replaced by the pro-Soviet José Méndez Cominches. This gave Moscow strong influence over Cuba's foreign spying during the Cold War, though the two services also competed. Russia's present services are its successors.
cite: Christopher Andrew and Vasili Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive; studies of Cuban intelligence; Markus Wolf, Man Without a Face (1997); Czech Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes (ÚSTR) histories of the StB

n: Beny Steinmetz

how.bsgr: Steinmetz is identified as BSGR's owner; Swiss prosecutors charged that he and associates paid about US$10 million to a wife of Guinea's president Lansana Conté to win Simandou iron-ore rights.

d: Beny Steinmetz is an Israeli diamond and mining billionaire identified as the owner of BSG Resources. In 2008 BSGR won rights to half of the Simandou iron-ore deposit in Guinea after they were taken from Rio Tinto, and later sold half of its stake to Vale for US$2.5 billion. Global Witness and an FBI case found bribery contracts with Mamadie Touré, a wife of the late president Lansana Conté. Swiss prosecutors charged that he and associates paid about US$10 million to win the rights, and he was put on trial in Geneva. Guinea stripped BSGR of the rights in 2014. He denies wrongdoing.
cite: Global Witness 'Guinea's deal of the century' (2014); Geneva prosecutors' indictment (2019); Mining.com

n: Þorsteinn Már Baldvinsson

how.samherji: Baldvinsson was Samherji's chief executive and biggest shareholder and is alleged to have authorised payments to Namibian officials for fishing quotas, revealed in the 2019 Fishrot Files.

d: Þorsteinn Már Baldvinsson co-founded and ran Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, and is its biggest shareholder. In November 2019 WikiLeaks, Al Jazeera and Icelandic media published the Fishrot Files, based on documents from a former Samherji manager. They showed payments of hundreds of millions of Icelandic krónur to people close to Namibia's fisheries and justice ministers in return for horse mackerel quotas. Both ministers resigned and were arrested with others. Baldvinsson is alleged to have authorised the payments and stepped aside as chief executive during an internal review. He denies wrongdoing.
cite: Fishrot Files (WikiLeaks, Al Jazeera, Stundin, Kveikur, Nov 2019); Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission

n: Gavin Watson and the Watson family

how.bosasa: Gavin Watson became chief executive in 1996 and bought Bosasa in 2000; the Zondo Commission found in 2022 that the company bribed politicians, officials and President Zuma as its way of doing business.

d: Gavin Watson, from a well-known anti-apartheid family in the Eastern Cape, became chief executive of the company that became Bosasa in 1996, after a deal with a trust controlled by the ANC Women's League, and bought it in 2000. Bosasa won about R12 billion in government tenders for prisons and other services between 2003 and 2018. Its former chief operating officer, Angelo Agrizzi, testified that cash was paid to ministers and officials. In 2022 the Zondo Commission found that Bosasa bribed politicians, officials and President Jacob Zuma, and that corruption was its way of doing business. Watson died in a car crash in 2019.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo), Part 3 report (Mar 2022)

n: Espírito Santo family (Espírito Santo Financial Group)

how.bes: The family's Luxembourg holding, Espírito Santo Financial Group, with Crédit Agricole controlled about 50.8% of Banco Espírito Santo from 1991; under family head Ricardo Salgado the bank collapsed in 2014.

d: The Espírito Santo family were one of Portugal's leading banking dynasties. After the bank was nationalised in 1975 they rebuilt their business through a holding company in Luxembourg, the Espírito Santo Financial Group. In 1991 they and France's Crédit Agricole retook control of Banco Espírito Santo, holding about 50.8%. Ricardo Salgado, of the family, ran the bank. In 2014 losses hidden in family companies brought it down; the state split it and put €4.9 billion into the new Novo Banco. The Bank of Portugal found the management had disobeyed it 21 times and practised ruinous management.
cite: Bank of Portugal resolution decision (3 Aug 2014) and administrative findings (2015)

n: Orbán government of Hungary (Fidesz) and the Mathias Corvinus Collegium foundation

how.mol: In 2011 the state bought back a 21.2% stake in MOL; in 2020 parliament gave 10% of MOL to the Mathias Corvinus Collegium foundation, chaired by Balázs Orbán, and a further 10% went to another state-created foundation.

d: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz government has kept a large hand in MOL, Hungary's oil and gas company. In 2011 the state bought back the 21.2% stake held by Russia's Surgutneftegas. In 2020 parliament transferred 10% of MOL, with other assets worth about US$1.7 billion in all, to the Mathias Corvinus Collegium foundation. Its board is chaired by Balázs Orbán who helped plan the transfer as a state secretary. Another state-created foundation, Maecenas Universitatis Corvini, holds a further 10%. This places shares of the country's largest company with bodies run by government allies.
cite: MOL shareholder register (31 Dec 2025); Hungarian Act on public-interest trust foundations (2020); MCC records

n: Wen Qiang (Chongqing police and justice chief)

how.chongqing_gangs: Wen Qiang, a former deputy police chief and head of Chongqing's justice bureau, took bribes to protect gangs; he was sentenced to death in April 2010 and executed, while his sister-in-law ran a syndicate that bribed police.

d: Wen Qiang was for years a deputy police commissioner in Chongqing and then head of the city's justice bureau. During the 2009 crackdown on organised crime, led by party chief Bo Xilai and police chief Wang Lijun, he was arrested. In April 2010 a Chongqing court sentenced him to death for taking bribes, rape and holding unexplained wealth, and he was executed in July 2010. More than 30 million yuan was recovered from him. His sister-in-law Xie Caiping, who ran gambling dens and a syndicate that bribed police, got 18 years. The case showed senior police protecting the gangs.
cite: Chongqing Fifth Intermediate People's Court verdict (14 Apr 2010); Xinhua

n: Ford family (Henry and Edsel Ford)

how.ford_foundation: Edsel Ford founded it on 15 January 1936 with a $25,000 gift; by 1947 it held 90% of Ford Motor's non-voting shares while the family kept the votes, and Henry Ford II sat on its board until 1976.

d: Henry Ford and his son Edsel built the Ford Motor Company. In 1936 Edsel set up the Ford Foundation in Michigan with $25,000. After both men died, the foundation received most of their Ford shares; by 1947 it owned 90% of the company's non-voting stock, while the family kept the voting shares and so kept control of the firm. This let the family pass on its fortune largely free of inheritance tax. The foundation became one of the richest in the world. It sold its Ford shares between 1955 and 1974, and the last family trustee, Henry Ford II, resigned in 1976.
cite: Wikipedia, Ford Foundation; Ford Foundation history

n: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (as WHO funder)

how.who: Was the WHO's second-largest contributor in 2020, giving 45% of its non-governmental money, about 12% of its total operating spending.

d: The Gates Foundation is the private charity of Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, and his former wife Melinda French Gates. By 2020 it was the second-largest funder of the World Health Organization after the United States. It supplied about 45% of the money the WHO got from non-governmental sources, or about 12% of the WHO's total spending. Most of this money is tied to programmes the foundation chooses, such as polio. Researchers and health charities have said this gives a single private donor outsized say over a body run by governments, which is possible because member states pay so little.
cite: Wikipedia, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; WHO funding records

n: International Olympic Committee (as WADA founder and funder)

how.wada: Led the 1999 founding of WADA with governments, paid its early costs, still pays half its budget and fills half the seats on its 38-member Foundation Board.

d: The International Olympic Committee runs the Olympic Games from Lausanne. In 1999, after doping scandals, it led the creation of the World Anti-Doping Agency together with more than 140 governments. The IOC paid for WADA at first and still pays half of its budget; governments pay the other half. Half of the seats on WADA's top body, the Foundation Board, go to the Olympic movement. Critics say this means the sports bodies that WADA is meant to police also pay for it and help run it, which became an issue when WADA handled Russia's state doping programme.
cite: Wikipedia, World Anti-Doping Agency; WADA governance pages

n: United States government (Treasury Department)

how.imf: Holds about 16.5% of IMF votes, enough to block any change needing an 85% majority; the Treasury Secretary is the US governor.
how.world_bank: Holds about 15.9% of IBRD votes, enough to block charter changes needing 85%, and by custom the US president picks every World Bank president.

d: The US Treasury speaks for the United States at the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, both based in Washington. Votes in these lenders follow how much money each country puts in. The US has the biggest share, about 16.5% at the IMF and about 15.9% at the World Bank's main lending arm. Because major changes need 85% of the votes, the US alone can block them. By an informal deal with Europe, the US president names the head of the World Bank and Europe names the head of the IMF. This gives Washington a steady hand in the loan conditions both bodies set for poorer countries.
cite: Wikipedia, International Monetary Fund; Wikipedia, World Bank Group; IMF and World Bank voting tables

n: The Coca-Cola Company (as ILSI founder)

how.ilsi: Coca-Cola senior vice-president Alex Malaspina founded ILSI in 1978, and Coca-Cola stayed a paying member until it withdrew in 2021.

d: Coca-Cola is the world's largest soft-drink company. In 1978 one of its senior vice-presidents, Alex Malaspina, founded the International Life Sciences Institute, a body that presents itself as a science group but is paid for mostly by member companies' dues (70.8% of its 2020 income). Members have included Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonald's, BASF and Syngenta. Researchers who studied the group, including Sarah Steele, said it should be seen as an industry group. In China ILSI worked closely with health officials, and nutrition experts say it helped keep the focus off sugary drinks. Coca-Cola left ILSI in 2021.
cite: Wikipedia, International Life Sciences Institute; The Guardian (2019); BMJ, Greenhalgh (2019)

n: Doug Barrowman and Baroness Michelle Mone

how.ppe_medpro: Mone put PPE Medpro into the government's 'VIP lane' in 2020; the High Court found in October 2025 that Barrowman 'appears to have been the economic principal of the business', and £29m from it reached a trust for Mone and her children.

d: Michelle Mone is a Conservative member of the House of Lords; Doug Barrowman, her husband, is a businessman based on the Isle of Man. In 2020 Mone recommended PPE Medpro to ministers through the 'VIP lane' for suppliers backed by politicians, and the firm won about £200 million in contracts. For years both denied any link. Leaked documents and a 2025 High Court judgment showed otherwise: the judge said Barrowman appeared to be the real owner, and £29 million had gone to a trust for Mone's family. The court ordered PPE Medpro to repay almost £122 million for faulty gowns.
cite: High Court judgment, DHSC v PPE Medpro (1 Oct 2025); Civil Service World (2 Oct 2025); The Guardian

n: Prince Alwaleed bin Talal (Kingdom Holding)

how.citigroup: Rescued Citicorp in 1991 with $590 million, rising to $797 million or about 15% of the bank, and stayed one of its largest shareholders for years.

d: Alwaleed bin Talal is a grandson of Saudi Arabia's founding king and runs the investment firm Kingdom Holding. In January 1991 Citicorp, then America's biggest bank, was short of capital after bad property loans. Alwaleed agreed to put in $590 million, about half his wealth, and by February his stake had reached $797 million, about 15% of the bank. He trimmed it below 10% in 1993 to stay under a Federal Reserve limit. Citigroup's later chief Sandy Weill said the money 'really saved the bank'. Alwaleed called the tie 'an alliance', and he kept a large stake for many years.
cite: Wikipedia, Alwaleed bin Talal; New York Times (1991)

n: Salva Kiir Mayardit (President of South Sudan)

how.bol_mel_companies: Kept Benjamin Bol Mel as his principal financial adviser, made him a vice-president on 10 February 2025 and removed him by decree on 12 November 2025; the US sanctioned Bol Mel in December 2017.

d: Salva Kiir has been president of South Sudan since independence in 2011. His long-time money man, Benjamin Bol Mel, ran construction and trading firms that won large state road contracts, many paid for but never built. Bol Mel served as Kiir's principal financial adviser, and in December 2017 the United States froze his assets under the Global Magnitsky Act for corruption. Kiir kept promoting him: in February 2025 he made him one of the country's vice-presidents and deputy leader of the ruling party, before sacking him in November 2025. The protection of the president is what let Bol Mel's companies keep winning state work.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designation (21 Dec 2017); Wikipedia, Benjamin Bol Mel; presidential decrees (2025)

n: Nuclear Damage Compensation and Decommissioning Facilitation Corporation (Japanese state fund)

how.tepco: Put ¥1 trillion into TEPCO in 2012 and has held 50.11% of its voting rights since, which it can raise to 88.69% by converting preferred shares.

d: After the Fukushima nuclear disaster in March 2011, the Japanese government created a state fund to pay victims and keep the Tokyo Electric Power Company running. In 2012 the fund put ¥1 trillion of public money into TEPCO and took 50.11% of its voting rights, with the option to go up to 88.69%. Since then TEPCO has in effect been owned by the Japanese state, which shapes its business plans and the clean-up. Critics say this puts the government on both sides of decisions about the disaster's costs and about restarting TEPCO's other nuclear plants.
cite: Wikipedia, Tokyo Electric Power Company; Japanese government announcements (2012)

n: Park Geun-hye government and the National Pension Service (South Korea)

how.samsung: Health minister Moon Hyung-pyo pushed the state pension fund, which held about 11% of Samsung C&T, to back the 2015 merger that tightened Lee Jae-yong's grip on Samsung; the Supreme Court upheld his 2.5-year sentence in April 2022.

d: In 2015 Samsung merged two of its companies, Samsung C&T and Cheil Industries, a deal that helped heir Lee Jae-yong take control of the group from his ailing father. The National Pension Service, a state fund holding about 11% of Samsung C&T, voted in favour, which carried the deal although critics said it was bad for pensioners. A special counsel later found that health minister Moon Hyung-pyo, in President Park Geun-hye's cabinet, had pressured the fund to back it without proper checks. He was jailed for two and a half years. The case formed part of the scandal that removed Park from office.
cite: Korea Times (14 Apr 2022); Supreme Court of Korea ruling; special counsel indictments (2017)

n: Chinese local government in Chengdu (CHJS co-founder)

how.chjs_tech: Set up CHJS (Chengdu Gaozhen) with ex-Samsung executive Choi in September 2020 and, Korean prosecutors say, put 400 billion won into it.

d: CHJS is a Chinese memory-chip company set up in September 2020 by a former Samsung Electronics and SK hynix executive named Choi, together with a Chinese local government. Korean prosecutors say the local government supplied 400 billion won, while Choi received shares worth 86 billion won. The firm hired former Samsung engineers and, prosecutors say, used Samsung's protected 20-nanometre DRAM process to make chips by April 2022, in about a year and a half instead of the usual four or five. Korean police valued the leaked technology at 4.3 trillion won. Choi and his chief designer were indicted in Seoul in 2024.
cite: Korea Times (10 Sep 2024); Asia Economy (27 Sep 2024); Seoul Central District Prosecutors' Office

n: Vinod Adani and associated offshore investors

how.adani: OCCRP reported in 2023 that two associates of Vinod Adani, Nasser Ali Shaban Ahli and Chang Chung-Ling, held 8-14% of four Adani companies through Mauritius funds, with trades coordinated with the family; the group denies it.

d: Vinod Adani is the Dubai-based elder brother of Gautam Adani, head of India's Adani Group. In August 2023 the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project reported that two men with long business ties to him, Nasser Ali Shaban Ahli from the UAE and Chang Chung-Ling from Taiwan, had held between 8% and 14% of the free-floating shares of four listed Adani companies through two Mauritius funds, worth $430 million at one point. If they were acting for the family, it would break India's rule that a quarter of shares must be held by the public. The Adani Group rejects the claims as baseless.
cite: OCCRP (31 Aug 2023); Financial Times; The Guardian; Al Jazeera (31 Aug 2023)

n: Jacob Zuma (President of South Africa 2009-2018)

how.gupta_network: The Zondo Commission found in 2022 that Zuma 'would do anything that the Guptas wanted him to do', firing finance minister Nene in 2015 and naming a Gupta-approved replacement; his son Duduzane was a director of Gupta firms.

d: Jacob Zuma met the Gupta brothers in 2003 and was president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018. His son Duduzane and daughter Duduzile sat on the boards of Gupta companies. The Zondo Commission into 'state capture' reported in 2022 that the Guptas had picked Zuma early as someone they could use, and that he did what they wanted: he sacked finance minister Nhlanhla Nene in 2015 shortly after a Gupta brother offered the job to his deputy, and he appointed people the Guptas approved. The commission found that Zuma, with ministers and board chairs, helped the family gain control at the state power company Eskom.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), Part IV-V (2022); Daily Maverick (30 Apr 2022)

n: Michael Yang (Yang Hong Ming), former economic adviser to Rodrigo Duterte

how.pharmally: Pharmally chairman Huang Tzu Yen told the Senate that Yang backed the firm's Chinese suppliers as funder and guarantor; the firm, with ₱625,000 paid-up capital, won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic contracts.

d: Michael Yang is a Chinese-born businessman in Davao who served as an economic adviser to President Rodrigo Duterte. In 2020 and 2021 Pharmally Pharmaceutical, a small firm with paid-up capital of just ₱625,000, won pandemic supply contracts worth billions of pesos from the government's procurement service. At Senate hearings Pharmally's own chairman said Yang had acted as funder and guarantor for its Chinese suppliers, which contradicted another director. Yang denied formal ties but admitted the firm asked him for help. The Senate Blue Ribbon draft report proposed charging Duterte over appointing Yang, though it never reached a full Senate vote.
cite: Philippine Senate Blue Ribbon Committee hearings (2021-22); Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism; Rappler

n: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and his son Mahmoud el-Sisi

how.egypt_gis: The GIS director is appointed by and reports to the president; Sisi placed his own chief of staff Abbas Kamel at its head in 2018 and his son Mahmoud is officially one of its two deputy directors.

d: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, a former army chief, has been Egypt's president since 2014. The General Intelligence Service answers directly to him, and he chooses its head. In 2018 he gave the post to Abbas Kamel, his long-time chief of staff, who led it until 2024. Sisi's son Mahmoud is officially one of the service's two deputy directors, and critics such as the exiled contractor Mohamed Ali say he is its real chief. Through a holding company, United Media Services, the GIS owns major TV channels and the newspaper Youm7, so the family's hold on the service reaches into Egypt's media.
cite: Wikipedia, General Intelligence Directorate (Egypt); Mada Masr reporting

n: Xinhua News Agency Hong Kong branch (CCP office in colonial Hong Kong)

how.hk_triads: In the early 1980s its official Wong Man-fong reportedly negotiated with Hong Kong triads on Beijing's behalf to keep the peace around the 1997 handover, part of a united front approach to the gangs.

d: Before 1997 the Chinese Communist Party ran its work in British Hong Kong through the local branch of the state news agency Xinhua, which acted as Beijing's unofficial embassy. One of its officials, Wong Man-fong, has said he negotiated with triad gangs in the early 1980s so that they would not disrupt the handover. Researchers such as former police officer Martin Purbrick argue the party saw triads as useful in its 'united front' work against opponents. Triad members took part in the July 2019 Yuen Long attack on democracy protesters. Beijing does not admit any formal tie to the triads.
cite: Wikipedia, Triad (organized crime); Martin Purbrick, Asian Affairs (2019); Washington Post

n: Rajapaksa brothers (Mahinda and Gotabaya Rajapaksa)

how.bbs: Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa opened the BBS training centre in Galle District on 9 March 2013 as chief guest; an opposition MP alleged the Defence Ministry secretly funded the group, which BBS denied.

d: Mahinda Rajapaksa was Sri Lanka's president from 2005 to 2015, and his brother Gotabaya ran the Defence Ministry before becoming president himself in 2019. Bodu Bala Sena, a Buddhist nationalist group led by monks, rose in 2012-13 with campaigns against Muslims. In January 2013 Mahinda met its leaders at his official residence, and in March 2013 Gotabaya was chief guest at the opening of its training centre near Galle. Opposition MP Mangala Samaraweera claimed the Defence Ministry was secretly funding it. Government pressure that followed BBS demands ended Muslim halal certification. Direct funding has not been proved.
cite: Wikipedia, Bodu Bala Sena (citing Daily Mirror and Sunday Times Sri Lanka, 2013)

n: Holy See (the Pope and the Roman Curia)

how.ior: Pius XII created the IOR by decree on 27 June 1942; it reports to a commission of five cardinals and the Pope, and since August 2022 must manage all the Holy See's money.
how.opus_dei: John Paul II made Opus Dei a 'personal prelature' in 1982, a worldwide diocese without territory; Francis put it under the Dicastery for the Clergy in 2022.
how.irish_catholic_hierarchy: In 1997 its nuncio wrote to Irish bishops that their 1996 rules on reporting child abuse to police were only a 'study document', which the 2011 Cloyne Report said gave cover to bishops who did not report.

d: The Holy See is the central government of the Catholic Church, headed by the Pope in Vatican City. It created the Vatican bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion, in 1942 and governs it through a commission of cardinals; since 2022 the bank must hold all the Holy See's assets. It also gave Opus Dei a status no other group has: in 1982 John Paul II made it a personal prelature, letting its own prelate oversee members in any country. Pope Francis cut that status back in 2022 and 2023. Papal decisions therefore shape both bodies' power.
cite: Papal decree of 27 June 1942; apostolic constitution Ut sit (1982); motu proprio Ad charisma tuendum (2022); Commission of Investigation, Report into the Catholic Diocese of Cloyne (July 2011); Enda Kenny, Dáil Éireann speech (20 July 2011)

n: Father Piotr Skarga Association and Foundation (Tradition, Family and Property network)

how.ordo_iuris: The Father Piotr Skarga Foundation founded Ordo Iuris in 2013 with 50,000 zloty; the association behind it says it is inspired by the Brazilian Tradition, Family and Property movement.

d: The Father Piotr Skarga Association is a Polish Catholic group that says it is inspired by Tradition, Family and Property, an ultra-conservative movement founded in Brazil in the 1960s by Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira, with branches across Europe and the Americas. Its foundation set up the Ordo Iuris legal institute in 2013 with 50,000 zloty. Ordo Iuris lawyers went on to draft bills, including a near-total abortion ban, and to take posts in Poland's state bodies under the Law and Justice government. Reporting by openDemocracy and the European Parliamentary Forum's 2018 report traced this chain.
cite: openDemocracy (Lidia Kurasinska); European Parliamentary Forum, 'Restoring the Natural Order' (2018); Polish court registry

n: Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines)

how.shinseiren: Set up Shinto Seiji Renmei on 8 November 1969 as its lobbying arm; the league's head office is inside Jinja Honcho's building in Shibuya.
how.nippon_kaigi: Shinto shrine priests and religious groups helped form Nippon Kaigi in 1997, and many of the shrine league's officers also hold Nippon Kaigi posts, with largely shared Diet caucuses.

d: Jinja Honcho is the body that groups about 80,000 Shinto shrines across Japan, based in Tokyo next to the Meiji Shrine. In 1969 it created a political arm, Shinto Seiji Renmei, which works from inside its headquarters and runs a caucus of Diet members, mostly from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. The shrine world also helped found the nationalist lobby Nippon Kaigi in 1997, and many officers sit on both. Through these bodies the shrines lobbied successfully for the 1999 flag-and-anthem law and the 2006 education law revision, and for prime ministers' visits to Yasukuni Shrine.
cite: Japanese Wikipedia, 神道政治連盟; Wikipedia, Association of Shinto Shrines; Wikipedia, Nippon Kaigi

n: Cecil Rhodes and his estate

how.society_of_elect: In an 1877 will Rhodes left his future fortune to found a secret society for the 'extension of British rule throughout the world'; Carroll Quigley traced the society to this plan.
how.rhodes_trust: His final will of July 1899 set up the Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford and the trust that pays for them.

d: Cecil Rhodes made a fortune from diamonds and gold in southern Africa and was prime minister of the Cape Colony. In 1877, before he was rich, he wrote a will leaving his money to found a secret society to spread British rule across the world. The historian Carroll Quigley later argued that this plan lived on as the Milner Group. Rhodes's last will, of 1899, used his estate to create the Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford, run by the Rhodes Trust. The trust's money later helped fund the Round Table journal, and its scholars went into government posts across the Empire and the United States.
cite: Wikipedia, Cecil Rhodes; Carroll Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (1981)

n: Alfred Milner (Viscount Milner)

how.milner_kindergarten: As High Commissioner in South Africa from 1901 he hand-picked young Oxford men and Colonial Office staff to rebuild the conquered Boer republics.
how.round_table: Supplied the idea for the Round Table in 1909, steered Rhodes Trust money to its journal as the Trust's chief manager, and left it £2,500 in 1921.

d: Alfred Milner was Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa during and after the Boer War. From 1901 he gathered a group of young Oxford graduates, later called 'Milner's Kindergarten', to run the conquered territory. Members such as Lionel Curtis, Philip Kerr and Geoffrey Dawson later became an ambassador, the editor of The Times and the founder of Chatham House. In 1909 the group became the Round Table movement, built on Milner's idea, to push for a federated British Empire. As chief manager of the Rhodes Trust, Milner helped fund its journal, and he left it a final sum in his will.
cite: Wikipedia, Milner's Kindergarten; Wikipedia, Round Table movement; Quigley (1981)

n: Sir Abe Bailey

how.round_table: Along with the Rhodes Trust, was the main funder of The Round Table journal from its first issue in November 1910.

d: Abe Bailey was a South African gold-mining magnate and a close ally of Cecil Rhodes and Alfred Milner. When Milner's young aides returned to England in 1909 and formed the Round Table movement to argue for a united British Empire, Bailey's money, together with the Rhodes Trust's, paid for its journal, The Round Table, first published in November 1910. The journal and the group's private meetings gave its members, many of whom held senior posts, a shared platform to shape imperial policy. Bailey later also gave money to the Royal Institute of International Affairs (Chatham House).
cite: Wikipedia, Milner's Kindergarten; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (1981)

n: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the AKP government (2002-2013)

how.gulen: From 2002 the AKP and the Gülen movement had a pact against the military and secular elite, under which the movement built up its people in the police, courts and civil service; the alliance broke in December 2013.

d: The Justice and Development Party (AKP) of Recep Tayyip Erdoğan took power in Turkey in 2002. It formed a pact with the Gülen movement, the network of the preacher Fethullah Gülen, against the army and the secular establishment. While the AKP ran the government, Gülen's followers built up a strong presence in the police, the courts and the civil service, and two served as AKP MPs. The alliance broke in 2012-13, and in December 2013 police and prosecutors linked to the movement opened corruption cases against AKP ministers. After the failed 2016 coup, Erdoğan's government purged tens of thousands of alleged Gülenists.
cite: Wikipedia, Gülen movement (citing academic studies)

n: Chinese government semiconductor investment funds

how.wingtech: Almost 30% of Wingtech's shares trace back through layers to a State Council commission and government-run chip funds; a state-owned investor's JAC Capital had first bought Nexperia from NXP in 2017 before Wingtech took it over in 2018 for $3.6 billion.

d: China's government has set up investment funds to buy and build chip companies. Wingtech, a phone maker, is partly owned through layers of holding companies by a State Council commission and these state chip funds, close to 30% in all. In 2017 JAC Capital, part of a state-owned investment company, bought NXP's standard-chips unit, renamed Nexperia, and Wingtech took it over in 2018 for $3.6 billion. In October 2025 the Dutch government seized control of Nexperia's governance, citing fears that chip know-how would move to China. China answered with an export ban that caused car-chip shortages in Europe.
cite: Wikipedia, Nexperia; NRC; Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs (Oct 2025)

n: Chiquita Brands International

how.auc: Paid the AUC paramilitaries about $1.7 million from 1997 to 2004, and kept paying more than $300,000 after the US Justice Department told it to stop.

d: Chiquita is a US banana company with plantations in Colombia's Urabá and Santa Marta regions. From 1997 to 2004 its Colombian arm paid the AUC paramilitary federation about $1.7 million, as the company admitted in a 2007 US guilty plea for paying a designated terrorist group; it paid a $25 million fine. The money flowed while the AUC was killing trade unionists and peasants in the banana zones. In June 2024 a federal jury in Florida found Chiquita liable for eight killings by the AUC and ordered $38.3 million in damages.
cite: US Department of Justice plea agreement (March 2007); US District Court, Southern District of Florida, jury verdict (June 2024)

n: HSBC (HSBC Mexico and HSBC Bank USA)

how.sinaloa: Its weak controls let at least $881 million in drug money, including Sinaloa Cartel proceeds, pass through HSBC Mexico and HSBC USA, as it admitted in 2012.
how.norte_del_valle: The same 2012 admission named proceeds of Colombia's Norte del Valle Cartel among the $881 million moved through the bank.

d: HSBC is one of the world's largest banks, based in London. In December 2012 it admitted to the US Justice Department that its Mexican and American arms had let at least $881 million in drug-trafficking money flow into the US financial system, including proceeds of the Sinaloa Cartel and Colombia's Norte del Valle Cartel. Cartel couriers deposited cash at HSBC Mexico branches, sometimes in boxes sized to fit teller windows. Clean bank accounts let the cartels pay suppliers, buy aircraft and bribe officials. HSBC paid $1.92 billion under a deferred prosecution agreement; no executive was charged.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 'HSBC Holdings plc and HSBC Bank USA N.A. admit anti-money laundering and sanctions violations' (11 Dec 2012); US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report (July 2012)

n: Genaro García Luna (Mexico's federal security chief, 2001-2012)

how.sinaloa: Took cash bribes from the Sinaloa Cartel while running Mexico's federal police and later the Public Security ministry; convicted in New York in February 2023.

d: Genaro García Luna headed Mexico's Federal Investigation Agency and then, from 2006 to 2012, the federal Public Security ministry that led President Calderón's drug war. A Brooklyn jury convicted him in February 2023 of taking bribes from the Sinaloa Cartel; at El Chapo Guzmán's 2018 trial a cartel witness said he had twice received suitcases holding $3 million. In return the cartel got protection and help against rivals from the police force he commanded. In October 2024 he was sentenced to 38 years, the highest Mexican official ever convicted in the United States.
cite: US Department of Justice, conviction (21 Feb 2023) and sentencing (16 Oct 2024), Eastern District of New York; testimony of Jesús Zambada García (2018)

n: Manuel Noriega (military ruler of Panama, 1983-1989)

how.medellin: Took protection payments to let the Medellín Cartel ship cocaine and launder money through Panama; convicted of drug trafficking and racketeering in Miami in 1992.

d: Manuel Noriega commanded Panama's armed forces and ran the country from 1983 until the US invasion of December 1989. He had also been a paid CIA asset. US prosecutors showed that he took bribes and shares of profits from the Medellín Cartel in exchange for letting it move cocaine through Panama and launder its money in Panamanian banks. Indicted by Florida grand juries in 1988, he was convicted on eight counts in April 1992 and sentenced to 40 years. His protection gave the cartel a safe transit country and banking centre.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of Florida, conviction (April 1992); Miami and Tampa grand jury indictments (1988)

n: Dirección Federal de Seguridad (DFS), Mexico's former political police

how.guadalajara: Protected the Guadalajara Cartel's leaders in the early 1980s; DFS agents took part in the 1985 kidnapping of DEA agent Enrique Camarena, and the agency was dissolved that year.

d: The DFS was Mexico's federal political police and intelligence agency from 1947 to 1985, answering to the Interior Ministry. Historians and later inquiries describe it as the protector of the Guadalajara Cartel, which grew from the plaza bosses the DFS managed in the late 1970s. DFS officers reportedly took part in the February 1985 kidnapping of US drug agent Enrique Camarena, who was tortured and killed at a house owned by cartel leader Rafael Caro Quintero. The scandal led the government to dissolve the DFS in November 1985. Its former chief José Antonio Zorrilla was later jailed for the murder of a journalist investigating these links.
cite: Sergio Aguayo, La Charola (2001); Peter Dale Scott and Jonathan Marshall, Cocaine Politics (1991); Mexican government dissolution of DFS (29 Nov 1985)

n: General Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo (Mexico's drug czar, 1996-1997)

how.juarez: As head of Mexico's anti-drug institute he took payments from Amado Carrillo Fuentes to protect the Juárez Cartel; arrested February 1997 and imprisoned.

d: Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo was a Mexican army general named in December 1996 to head the National Institute to Combat Drugs, the country's top drug-fighting post. Ten weeks later he was arrested. Investigators held a recording of him discussing payments with Amado Carrillo Fuentes, leader of the Juárez Cartel, and found he lived in a flat he could not afford. In exchange he turned his forces against the cartel's rivals and left Carrillo's network alone. He was sentenced to about 31 years, with a further 40 added in 2007, and died in custody in 2013.
cite: Mexican federal court sentences (1997, 2007); New York Times, 'Mexico's Antidrug Chief Held on Charges He Protected Cartel' (19 Feb 1997)

n: Osiel Cárdenas Guillén (Gulf Cartel leader, 1997-2003)

how.los_zetas: Created Los Zetas from 1999 by hiring army special-forces deserter Arturo Guzmán Decena, who recruited more than 30 other GAFE deserters as the Gulf Cartel's armed wing.

d: Osiel Cárdenas Guillén took over the Gulf Cartel in 1997. To protect himself from rivals and the army he hired Arturo Guzmán Decena, a deserter from Mexico's army special forces (GAFE), in 1999. Guzmán recruited more than thirty fellow deserters, and this paid bodyguard unit became Los Zetas, named after his radio code 'Z1'. The Gulf Cartel used them for kidnapping, extortion and securing smuggling routes. After Cárdenas's arrest in 2003 and extradition in 2007 the Zetas grew stronger and in 2010 broke away to become a cartel of their own.
cite: US Department of Justice, Cárdenas Guillén sentencing (Feb 2010); InSight Crime, 'Zetas' profile

n: Government of Rwanda (Rwanda Defence Force and presidential circle)

how.cndp: Allowed recruitment for the CNDP on Rwandan soil, supplied it, and had officers in phone contact with its leaders, according to the UN Group of Experts report of December 2008.

d: Rwanda's government, led by Paul Kagame and the Rwandan Patriotic Front, backed the CNDP rebel movement of Laurent Nkunda in eastern Congo. A UN Group of Experts report in December 2008 found that recruits, including children, were enlisted in Rwanda, moved to the border in Rwandan army trucks, and that CNDP leaders kept bank accounts in Rwanda and held phone contact with Rwandan army and presidential officials. A presidential adviser, Tribert Rujugiro, was named as a key financier. Netherlands and Sweden suspended aid. Rwanda then arrested Nkunda in January 2009 in a deal with Kinshasa.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the DRC, final report S/2008/773 (12 Dec 2008)

n: Government of Eritrea (Isaias Afwerki)

how.al_shabaab: Gave money, arms and training to Somali Islamist fighters including al-Shabaab around 2007-2009, for which the UN Security Council imposed sanctions in Resolution 1907 (December 2009).

d: Eritrea has been ruled by President Isaias Afwerki since independence in 1993. After Ethiopia invaded Somalia in 2006, Eritrea backed Somali Islamist forces fighting Ethiopia. The UN Monitoring Group on Somalia reported Eritrean payments, arms and training, and in December 2009 the Security Council imposed an arms embargo and travel bans on Eritrea in Resolution 1907 for aiding al-Shabaab. From 2012 the same monitors said they found no evidence of direct support, and Eritrea denied the charge throughout. The sanctions were lifted in November 2018 after peace with Ethiopia.
cite: UN Security Council Resolution 1907 (23 Dec 2009); UN Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea reports (2010-2017); UNSC Resolution 2444 (Nov 2018)

n: Dagalo family (Hemedti and his brothers) and its Al Junaid company

how.rsf_sudan: Commands the RSF and funds it through family companies such as Al Junaid gold, run by deputy commander Abdel Rahim Dagalo; the US sanctioned Hemedti and seven UAE-based RSF companies in January 2025.

d: Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, called Hemedti, leads the Rapid Support Forces, and his brother Abdel Rahim is deputy commander. The family runs the RSF almost as a business: Abdel Rahim heads Al Junaid, a company with gold mines in Darfur, and another brother, Algoney, controls front companies in Dubai. Global Witness traced close financial links between Al Junaid and the RSF, with gold exported to the United Arab Emirates. This money pays fighters and buys weapons and vehicles without depending on the state. The US Treasury sanctioned Al Junaid in 2023 and Hemedti himself in January 2025.
cite: Global Witness, 'Exposing the RSF's secret financial network' (2019); US Treasury sanctions (June 2023, January 2025)

n: Omar al-Bashir's government and the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS), Sudan

how.rsf_sudan: Created the RSF in August 2013 by reorganising Janjaweed militias under the NISS intelligence service, and later gave it legal status answering to the presidency.

d: Omar al-Bashir ruled Sudan from 1989 until 2019 with an Islamist military government. To fight rebels in Darfur and the south without relying on the army, his government reorganised the Janjaweed militias in August 2013 into the Rapid Support Forces, first placed under the National Intelligence and Security Service and later, by a 2017 law, answering to the president himself. Bashir called Hemedti 'my protection'. The arrangement gave the RSF state salaries, weapons and legal cover, which let it grow into a rival army that helped remove Bashir in 2019 and went to war with the army in 2023.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Men With No Mercy' (2015); Sudan Rapid Support Forces Act (2017)

n: Muammar Gaddafi's Libyan government

how.ira: Shipped the Provisional IRA weapons and Semtex explosive in the 1970s and 1980s; the fifth ship, the Eksund, was seized off France in 1987 carrying about 150 tonnes of Libyan-donated arms.

d: Muammar Gaddafi ruled Libya from 1969 to 2011 and backed armed groups he saw as fighting Western powers. He supplied the Provisional IRA with money and weapons in the 1970s and, after Britain let US jets use its bases to bomb Libya in 1986, sent several shiploads of rifles, machine guns, rocket launchers and Semtex plastic explosive. Four ships got through in 1985-86; the Eksund, carrying about 150 tonnes, was seized off France in 1987, and its captain revealed the earlier runs. The Libyan arsenal let the IRA keep up its campaign until the 1990s.
cite: Ed Moloney, A Secret History of the IRA (2002); French customs seizure of the Eksund (Oct 1987); UK government statements

n: Irish Northern Aid Committee (NORAID)

how.ira: Raised up to $3 million in the US from 1970 to 1985; a US federal judge ruled in 1981 that it acted as an agent of the IRA and had to register it as its foreign principal.

d: NORAID was founded in New York in 1969 by Michael Flannery, a veteran of the IRA in the 1920s, to raise money among Irish Americans. It said its money went to families of republican prisoners. The British, Irish and US governments said much of it bought weapons for the Provisional IRA. In May 1981 a US district judge ruled that NORAID was acting as an agent of the IRA and must register it under the Foreign Agents Registration Act; NORAID lost its appeal. It raised up to $3 million between 1970 and 1985. Some historians dispute how much went to arms.
cite: US District Court ruling under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (May 1981); Brian Hanley, 'The Politics of Noraid', Irish Political Studies (2004)

n: Force Research Unit (FRU), British Army intelligence

how.uvf: Ran Brian Nelson as its agent and helped him become the UDA's chief intelligence officer, where he passed on targets; the Stevens and de Silva inquiries found collusion, including in the 1989 murder of Pat Finucane.

d: The Force Research Unit was a secret British Army unit that ran informers inside armed groups in Northern Ireland during the Troubles. It recruited Brian Nelson, a loyalist, and helped him become chief intelligence officer of the Ulster Defence Association, which kept files on people to be killed. Instead of stopping attacks, the unit's handlers let many go ahead. The Stevens inquiries found that the FRU colluded with loyalist paramilitaries and saved far fewer lives than it claimed, and Sir Desmond de Silva's 2012 report found state collusion in the 1989 murder of solicitor Pat Finucane. Prime Minister David Cameron apologised.
cite: Stevens Inquiry reports (1990, 1994, 2003); Sir Desmond de Silva, The Report of the Patrick Finucane Review (Dec 2012)

n: Saddam Hussein's Iraqi government

how.mek: Hosted the MEK at Camp Ashraf from 1986, and armed and paid its National Liberation Army, which fought Iran alongside Iraq in 1988.

d: Saddam Hussein ruled Iraq from 1979 to 2003 and fought Iran from 1980 to 1988. In 1983 MEK leader Massoud Rajavi met Iraqi deputy prime minister Tariq Aziz, and in 1986, after France expelled the group, the MEK moved its fighters to Iraq. Saddam's government gave it a large base, Camp Ashraf, and armed and supplied its National Liberation Army, formed in 1987, which attacked Iran in July 1988. The US State Department describes Iraq as the MEK's main backer in this period. Iraqi support lasted until the 2003 invasion.
cite: US State Department, Country Reports on Terrorism; RAND Corporation, 'The Mujahedin-e Khalq in Iraq: A Policy Conundrum' (2009)

n: Sri Lankan security forces (army and police) under the Rajapaksa government

how.tmvp: Worked with the Karuna faction against the Tamil Tigers after 2004; Human Rights Watch documented TMVP child abductions done near army camps and with army complicity in 2006.

d: After Karuna Amman broke from the Tamil Tigers in 2004, Sri Lanka's army and police worked with his faction, later the TMVP, as an ally in the east. Human Rights Watch reported in 2007 that the group forcibly recruited hundreds of children in 2006, holding some opposite a military camp, and said this could not happen without army complicity; TMVP fighters manned army checkpoints. The alliance gave the government a Tamil armed group to fight the Tigers and later to win provincial elections in 2008. Karuna was made a government minister in 2009. Sri Lanka denied directing the abuses.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Complicit in Crime: State Collusion in Abductions and Child Recruitment by the Karuna Group' (Jan 2007); UN Special Representative Allan Rock report (Nov 2006)

n: Eugène Schueller (L'Oréal) and allied French industrialists

how.la_cagoule: Schueller, founder of L'Oréal, with Louis Renault and Jacques Lemaigre-Dubreuil, financed the Cagoule's secret army in 1936-37; Fascist Italy supplied arms after the group murdered the anti-fascist Rosselli brothers.

d: La Cagoule was a secret French far-right group founded in 1936 by Eugène Deloncle to overthrow the Popular Front government. Its money came from wealthy industrialists, among them Eugène Schueller, founder of the cosmetics firm L'Oréal, carmaker Louis Renault and oil businessman Jacques Lemaigre-Dubreuil. The funds paid for weapons depots, bombings staged to look like communist attacks, and a planned coup that police broke up in November 1937. The group also murdered the Italian anti-fascist Rosselli brothers in June 1937, which helped it get arms from Mussolini's Italy. The funding came out in police investigations and the 1948 trial.
cite: Cagoule trial records (Paris, 1948); Michael Bar-Zohar, Bitter Scent (1996); Philippe Bourdrel, La Cagoule (1970)

n: Nazi Germany (Hitler's government, the SS and the Foreign Office)

how.arrow_cross: Put Arrow Cross leader Ferenc Szálasi in power in October 1944 through Operation Panzerfaust, abducting Horthy's son and forcing Horthy to abdicate.
how.iron_guard: The SS and its SD intelligence service funded and armed the Iron Guard, sheltered its leaders after 1938 and 1941, and helped Horia Sima rise to lead it.
how.golden_square: Gave the Golden Square colonels' 1941 government diplomatic recognition and sent Luftwaffe aircraft to fight the British in Iraq.

d: Hitler's Germany backed fascist movements across Europe and the Middle East to gain allies. The SS and Alfred Rosenberg's foreign office paid Romania's Iron Guard and sheltered its leaders after the king crushed it in 1938 and again after its failed revolt in 1941. In October 1944, when Hungary's regent Horthy tried to leave the war, German commandos seized his son and forced him to hand power to the Arrow Cross, which then deported and murdered tens of thousands of Jews. In 1941 Germany recognised and armed Iraq's Golden Square officers against Britain.
cite: Rebecca Haynes, 'Germany and the Establishment of the Romanian National Legionary State', Slavonic and East European Review (1999); Randolph Braham, The Politics of Genocide (1981); German Foreign Office records

n: Ihor Kolomoisky

how.azov: Was the main financier of the Azov Battalion in 2014 while governor of Dnipropetrovsk region, before it was folded into the National Guard.

d: Ihor Kolomoisky is a Ukrainian billionaire who co-owned PrivatBank and was governor of Dnipropetrovsk region in 2014-15. When Russia-backed forces seized parts of the Donbas in 2014, he paid for several volunteer battalions, spending a reported $10 million on the Dnipro Battalion and also funding Aidar, Donbas and Azov. Researchers name him as Azov's main early financier. The money let a unit founded by far-right activist Andriy Biletsky arm itself before the state took it into the National Guard in November 2014. Kolomoisky was later charged with fraud over PrivatBank and arrested in Ukraine in 2023.
cite: Andreas Umland, 'Irregular Militias and Radical Nationalism in Post-Euromaydan Ukraine', Terrorism and Political Violence (2019); Reuters and Ukrainian press (2014)

n: Israeli government ministries and the World Zionist Organization Settlement Division

how.settler_movement: Spent state money on settlements and outposts that were illegal even under Israeli law: the Housing Ministry supplied 400 mobile homes and the WZO Settlement Division channelled funds, the 2005 Sasson Report found.

d: Israeli governments since 1967 have paid for much of the settler movement's growth in the occupied West Bank. A report ordered by Prime Minister Sharon and written by former state prosecutor Talia Sasson in March 2005 found that the Housing Ministry, the Defence Ministry and the Settlement Division of the World Zionist Organization had quietly spent millions of shekels on outposts that lacked even Israeli legal approval. The Housing Ministry supplied 400 mobile homes, the Education Ministry paid for nurseries and the Energy Ministry connected outposts to the grid. Sasson called it a blatant violation of the law.
cite: Talia Sasson, Opinion Concerning Unauthorized Outposts, report to the Prime Minister of Israel (8 March 2005)

n: Hugo Chávez's Venezuelan government (military intelligence, DISIP and Interior Ministry)

how.farc: Senior officials gave the FARC weapons, Venezuelan identity papers and protection for drug shipments, and the interior minister tried to arrange a $250 million loan, the US Treasury found in September 2008.

d: Hugo Chávez governed Venezuela from 1999 to 2013. Files from the laptop of FARC commander Raúl Reyes, seized by Colombia in 2008 and found by Interpol not to have been tampered with, pointed to Venezuelan help for the guerrillas. In September 2008 the US Treasury sanctioned three of Chávez's top officials: military intelligence chief Hugo Carvajal, accused of protecting FARC drug shipments and supplying arms and ID papers; intelligence chief Henry Rangel Silva; and former interior minister Ramón Rodríguez Chacín, called the government's main weapons contact for the FARC. Venezuela rejected the charges.
cite: US Treasury press release HP-1132 (12 Sept 2008); IISS, The FARC Files: Venezuela, Ecuador and the Secret Archive of Raúl Reyes (2011); Interpol forensic report (May 2008)

n: Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) leadership in West Kingston

how.shower_posse: Used the Shower Posse as its enforcer in the Tivoli Gardens garrison; Prime Minister Bruce Golding, the area's MP, resisted the US extradition request for leader Christopher Coke in 2009-10 and approved a JLP lobbying contract against it.

d: The Jamaica Labour Party has held the West Kingston seat, which includes the Tivoli Gardens housing scheme, since the 1960s under Edward Seaga and then Bruce Golding. The Shower Posse, founded by Lester Coke, served as the party's enforcer there, delivering votes and keeping order in exchange for protection. When the United States sought to extradite his son Christopher 'Dudus' Coke in 2009, Golding's government refused for nine months, and the JLP hired the US law firm Manatt, Phelps & Phillips to lobby against it. Public outcry forced a reversal; the May 2010 raid on Tivoli killed 76 people.
cite: Commission of Enquiry into the Extradition Request for Christopher Coke (Manatt enquiry), report (June 2011); Western Kingston Commission of Enquiry report (2016); FARA filing by Manatt, Phelps & Phillips (2009)

n: Halliburton

how.kbr: Owned KBR from its 1998 takeover of Dresser Industries until 2007, the years of the Nigerian bribery and the Iraq war contracts; it paid $382 million of the $402 million Nigeria bribery penalty.

d: Halliburton is a Houston oil-services company. It acquired KBR when it bought Dresser Industries in 1998, while Dick Cheney was its chief executive (1995-2000). As a Halliburton subsidiary, KBR paid bribes to Nigerian officials from 1994 to 2004 to win work on the Bonny Island gas plant, and became the largest US government contractor in Iraq after Cheney became vice-president. Halliburton spun KBR off in 2007. In 2009 the two firms paid $402 million to settle the US bribery case, of which Halliburton paid $382 million.
cite: US Department of Justice, KBR guilty plea and Halliburton settlement (Feb 2009); US SEC complaint (2009)

n: Bank of America

how.countrywide: Bought Countrywide in July 2008 for about $4 billion in stock, taking on its liabilities, and in 2014 paid nearly $17 billion largely over Countrywide's mortgage securities.
how.merrill_lynch: Agreed to buy Merrill Lynch for about $50 billion on 14 September 2008 under pressure from federal officials, completing the deal in January 2009.

d: Bank of America, based in Charlotte, North Carolina, is one of the largest US banks. During the 2008 financial crisis it bought two firms on the map: Countrywide Financial, the biggest subprime mortgage lender, in July 2008, and the investment bank Merrill Lynch, agreed the same weekend Lehman Brothers collapsed and completed in January 2009. Its chief executive told Congress federal officials pressed the Merrill deal through, and the bank received government bailout money. Owning both made it responsible for their past conduct, and in August 2014 it paid nearly $17 billion to settle claims, many over Countrywide's mortgage securities.
cite: Bank of America and Countrywide merger filings (2008); US Department of Justice settlement (21 Aug 2014); House Oversight Committee hearing (June 2009)

n: Lilly Endowment

how.eli_lilly: Founded in 1937 with Eli Lilly and Company shares by the Lilly family, it remains the drugmaker's largest shareholder and holds its assets mainly in Lilly stock.

d: The Lilly Endowment is a private foundation set up in Indianapolis in 1937 by Josiah K. Lilly Sr. and his sons with a gift of shares in the family drug company, Eli Lilly and Company. Its wealth is still mostly Lilly stock, which makes it the company's largest shareholder, with 92.5 million shares in its latest filing. As Lilly's share price soared on weight-loss drugs, the endowment's assets passed about $100 billion in November 2025. The stake gives it a lasting voice in the company's control.
cite: Lilly Endowment annual reports; Eli Lilly and Company proxy statements (SEC filings); Bloomberg, 25 November 2025

n: Steven Mnuchin and the IMB HoldCo investor group

how.onewest: Led the seven-member group that bought the failed IndyMac from the FDIC in March 2009 and renamed it OneWest, with FDIC loss-sharing that paid over $1 billion, then served as its chairman.

d: Steven Mnuchin, a former Goldman Sachs partner, led a group of investors called IMB HoldCo, including John Paulson, J. C. Flowers, Michael Dell's fund and George Soros, that bought the collapsed IndyMac Bank from the US deposit insurer in March 2009 and renamed it OneWest. The deal included a loss-sharing agreement under which the FDIC paid OneWest more than $1 billion by 2014. OneWest became known for foreclosing on tens of thousands of homeowners. The group sold it to CIT for $3.4 billion in 2015, and Mnuchin became US Treasury Secretary in 2017.
cite: FDIC press release on IndyMac sale (19 March 2009); FDIC records released 2016; Los Angeles Times (Aug 2015)

n: Angelini group (Empresas Copec and AntarChile)

how.corpesca: Owns about 77% of Corpesca through its holding companies; Corpesca's manager paid Senator Jaime Orpis while the 2012 fisheries law that gave quotas to a few families was passed.

d: The Angelini family, now led by Roberto Angelini, controls one of Chile's largest business groups through AntarChile and Empresas Copec, spanning fuel, forestry and fishing. It owns about 77% of Corpesca, the main fishing company in northern Chile. Prosecutors showed that Corpesca's general manager paid Senator Jaime Orpis about 230 million pesos through false invoices while Congress passed the 2012 'Longueira law', which handed fishing quotas indefinitely to a handful of families. Orpis was convicted in 2021 and jailed. Roberto Angelini told prosecutors he did not know of the payments.
cite: Chilean Fiscalía and Santiago Oral Criminal Court, Corpesca case ruling (2021); Diario Financiero (2015)

n: Kōnosuke Matsushita (founder of Panasonic)

how.matsushita_institute: Founded the institute in 1979 and endowed it from his personal fortune to train future politicians.

d: Kōnosuke Matsushita built the electronics company now called Panasonic and became one of Japan's richest men. In 1979, aged 84, he founded the Matsushita Institute of Government and Management at Chigasaki and paid for it from his personal capital, saying Japan needed a new kind of leader. Students live and train there for several years at no cost. By 2006, 66 of its 213 graduates had won elected office, and its alumni include prime ministers Yoshihiko Noda and Sanae Takaichi. His endowment created a private pipeline into the Diet that runs across party lines.
cite: Matsushita Institute of Government and Management official history; Japan Times reports on alumni

n: Gospel Outreach church (Eureka, California)

how.verbo: Its missionaries founded the Church of the Word (El Verbo) in Guatemala after the 1976 earthquake, and the church remained its affiliate when member Efraín Ríos Montt took power in 1982.

d: Gospel Outreach was a charismatic church from Eureka in northern California. Its members went to Guatemala after the 1976 earthquake to do relief work and set up Iglesia El Verbo, the Church of the Word, as an affiliate. General Efraín Ríos Montt joined it in 1978. When he seized power in March 1982, El Verbo elders served as his advisers, and the church helped organise US evangelical support for his government while the army carried out massacres of Maya villages. In 2013 a Guatemalan court convicted Ríos Montt of genocide; the verdict was later annulled.
cite: Virginia Garrard-Burnett, Terror in the Land of the Holy Spirit (2010); David Stoll, Is Latin America Turning Protestant? (1990)

n: Suharto (president of Indonesia, 1967-1998)

how.icmi: Permitted ICMI's founding in December 1990 under his minister B. J. Habibie and gave it patronage, so its members were placed in ministries and the civil service.

d: Suharto ruled Indonesia from 1967 to 1998 with army and Golkar party support. By 1990 he was courting Muslim opinion to balance the army, and he allowed his research minister B. J. Habibie to found the Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI) that December. With Suharto's patronage, ICMI members were placed in the civil service and cabinet, and the association set up the newspaper Republika. ICMI became Habibie's power base, which helped him become vice-president in 1998 and president when Suharto fell that May.
cite: Robert Hefner, Civil Islam (2000); Adam Schwarz, A Nation in Waiting (1999)

n: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial government (Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf)

how.haqqania: Gave Darul Uloom Haqqania Rs 300 million in its June 2016 budget and approved a further Rs 277 million grant in 2018.

d: Imran Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province from 2013. In its June 2016 budget the provincial government granted Rs 300 million (about $2.8 million) to Darul Uloom Haqqania, the seminary at Akora Khattak where many Afghan Taliban leaders studied, and in 2018 it approved Rs 277 million more. The province said the money was for mainstreaming religious schools. The seminary's head, Sami ul Haq, was a PTI political ally. Critics, including Asif Ali Zardari, said public money was going to a school known for training militants.
cite: Dawn, 'Haqqania funding: buck stops with CM' (June 2016); Dawn, 'KP govt to approve Rs277m grant for Darul Uloom Haqqania' (2018); Geo News (2016)

n: Juan Ponce Enrile (Philippine defence minister, 1970-1986)

how.ram_philippines: Was RAM's patron: its leader Gregorio Honasan was his security chief, and RAM planned the 1986 coup against Marcos under his leadership.

d: Juan Ponce Enrile was Ferdinand Marcos's defence minister. The Reform the Armed Forces Movement, founded in 1982 by young officers, grew up inside his ministry: its leader, Colonel Gregorio Honasan, headed Enrile's security, and RAM planned a coup under Enrile to remove Marcos in February 1986. When Marcos discovered the plot, Enrile and General Fidel Ramos held out in their camps and the People Power uprising followed. RAM later launched several coup attempts against President Corazon Aquino. Enrile's backing gave the officers protection and a route to power.
cite: Alfred McCoy, Closer Than Brothers (1999); Philippine Fact-Finding Commission (Davide Commission) report (1990)

n: Tōyama Mitsuru and the Genyōsha

how.black_dragon: Tōyama's Genyōsha was the parent of the Black Dragon Society, founded in 1901 by his protégé Uchida Ryōhei; Tōyama was a founder and at one time its head.

d: Tōyama Mitsuru was a nationalist leader from Fukuoka who co-founded the Genyōsha secret society in 1881 to push Japanese expansion into Asia. His follower Uchida Ryōhei founded the Black Dragon Society in 1901 as its successor, and Tōyama was a founder and for a time its head. Through his ties to politicians, army officers and businessmen he gave the society access and protection. It funded Asian revolutionaries such as Sun Yat-sen and gathered intelligence for the army in Korea and Manchuria. Tōyama stayed an influential power broker until his death in 1944.
cite: E. Herbert Norman, 'The Genyosha: A Study in the Origins of Japanese Imperialism', Pacific Affairs (1944); Joël Joos, studies of Tōyama Mitsuru

n: Lynde and Harry Bradley Foundation

how.pnac: Gave grants to the Project for the New American Century and its parent, the New Citizenship Project.

d: The Bradley Foundation in Milwaukee is one of the largest conservative grant-makers in the United States, built on the fortune of the Allen-Bradley electronics company. It funded the Project for the New American Century, the Washington group founded in 1997 by William Kristol and Robert Kagan, alongside the Scaife and Olin foundations. PNAC's 1998 letter urged removing Saddam Hussein, and ten of the 25 signers of its founding statement, including Dick Cheney, Donald Rumsfeld and Paul Wolfowitz, later served in George W. Bush's administration. Grants like Bradley's paid the staff and publications that carried these ideas.
cite: Media Transparency grant records; IRS Form 990 filings; Project for the New American Century records

n: United Front Department of the Workers' Party of Korea

how.chongryon: Directs Chongryon through its liaison staff, and North Korea paid about 46 billion yen in education aid to Chongryon schools over 50 years, while Chongryon businesses sent hard currency to Pyongyang.

d: The United Front Department is the branch of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party that handles South Korea and Koreans abroad. Chongryon, the association of pro-Pyongyang Koreans in Japan, works as North Korea's unofficial embassy there, and a former Japanese intelligence official said in 2014 that it is controlled by the department's liaison section. North Korea paid about 46 billion yen in 'educational aid' to Chongryon schools over fifty years, and Chongryon businesses, including pachinko parlours, sent hard currency back, estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars a year at the peak. Funds and orders flowed both ways.
cite: Japan Public Security Intelligence Agency annual reports; Mitsuhiro Suganuma interview (2014); Sonia Ryang, North Koreans in Japan (1997)

n: Daniel arap Moi's government and the KANU ruling party, Kenya

how.goldenberg: Granted Goldenberg a gold-export monopoly in 1990 and an extra 15% export subsidy; Moi personally authorised a KSh 5.8 billion payment in 1993, and the 2006 Bosire Commission recommended charging his finance minister.

d: Daniel arap Moi ruled Kenya from 1978 to 2002 through the KANU party. In 1990 his government gave Kamlesh Pattni's Goldenberg International a monopoly on gold exports and, through finance minister George Saitoti, 15% extra compensation on top of the legal 20%. Goldenberg claimed payments for gold that was largely never exported, and the money was allegedly passed to KANU before the 1992 elections. Pattni said Moi held shares through a nominee. The 2006 Bosire Commission found KSh 158 billion moved through the scheme and recommended charges against Saitoti and further investigation of Moi. The loss equalled over 10% of Kenya's GDP.
cite: Report of the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into the Goldenberg Affair (Bosire Commission, Feb 2006)
